stories.title: Why use family words with strangers?
stories.dek: In Vietnamese there is no neutral “you”. Every time you speak to someone, you choose a family word that places you both: older sister, uncle, grandchild.

sections.text: People are usually addressed with family words that reflect age and relationship.

sections.heading: The terms you will hear most
sections.text: Anh, chị, em, cô, chú and bác cover most everyday encounters.

sections.heading: A first name on its own
sections.text: Use a family word with the given name; the name alone can sound rude.

sections.heading: When you are not sure
sections.text: “Bạn ơi” works with people your age, and asking is always polite.

stories.appliesTo: Spoken Vietnamese in Hà Nội and the North. Most of it holds across the country; regional differences are marked.
stories.varies: Terms depend on age and relationship, and families and regions differ. Follow the word a person uses about themself.

paras.text: Buy a bunch of flowers from a woman about your mother’s age and you will not call her “you”. You will call her *cô*, aunt, and yourself *cháu*, her niece or nephew. She will answer the same way. A minute later, buying coffee from a student, you are *anh* or *chị*, older brother or sister, and the student is *em*.

Vietnamese has no neutral, all-purpose word for “you”, and even “I” is usually a family word. Speakers place themselves and the other person by age, relationship and status every time they open their mouth. It is less complicated than it sounds, and getting it roughly right is one of the warmest things a visitor can do.

paras.text: The key is that the words come in pairs. If you call a man *bác*, you are his *cháu*; if he calls you *em*, he is your *anh*. A Hà Nội linguist, Nguyễn Quang, shows how the pair carries the relationship: using both halves, “*cháu* invites *bác* upstairs”, sounds respectful even in a request, while dropping one half sounds closer and more relaxed.

This is everyday speech, not formality. In one survey, three quarters of responses used kinship words; in 500 recorded market conversations across four cities, buyers and sellers used them in 80% of their questions.

paras.text: To get someone’s attention, add *ơi* to the family word: *chị ơi* to a waitress a little older than you, *em ơi* to a younger one, *chú ơi* to a motorbike-taxi driver of your father’s generation, *bác ơi* to an older shopkeeper. It is the polite way to call someone over, in a restaurant, a market or the street, and it is far warmer than a wave or a raised finger.

If you cannot judge someone’s age at all, the tourism authority’s fallback is *bạn ơi*, “hey, friend”. It works well with people about your own age; with someone obviously older, choose *anh*, *chị* or *cô* and err on the generous side.

The words were family words first, and inside the family they are precise. *Bác* is a parent’s older brother or sister; *chú* is your father’s younger brother and *cô* his younger sister; *cậu* is your mother’s younger brother and *dì* her younger sister. That is why northern speakers, who use *chú* and *cô* for strangers of their parents’ age, rarely call an unrelated woman *dì*.

Regions differ even here. A Hà Nội child says *bố* and *mẹ*; a southern child often says *ba* and *má*. In the North the eldest brother is *anh cả* and *anh hai* is the second; in the South *anh hai* is the eldest. A northern great-grandparent is *cụ*, a southern one *cố*.

Phrasebooks often teach *tôi* for “I” and *bạn* for “you”. They are not wrong, but they are not neutral either. *Tôi* is the most impersonal word for oneself, polite but distant, and it once meant a king’s subject. *Bạn* means friend and fits people of about your own age. Researchers note that learners who use *tôi* and *bạn* with everyone can sound stiff, as two middle-aged neighbours would if they spoke that way.

Between friends of the same age, people use other pairs: *bạn* and *mình*, or the casual northern *tớ* and *cậu*. *Mày* and *tao* are for close friends at best and insults at worst; older Hà Nội families banned them at home.

Because the words depend on age, people often ask how old you are soon after meeting. It is not nosy: it is how both of you find the right pair. If you are not sure, it is fine to ask the person what you should call them: *Tôi nên gọi bạn thế nào ạ?*
And always put the family word before the given name, not the surname: *chị Lan*, *bác Nam*. The given name on its own can sound rude to someone older.

stories.title: Calling people with “ơi”
stories.dek: No “excuse me”, no raised hand: in Hà Nội you call people by a family word and a short “ơi”, and answer with “dạ”. A guide to getting attention, asking and replying politely.

sections.text: People call each other with a family word that matches the other person’s age, followed by “ơi”.

sections.heading: The safe choice
sections.text: If you are not sure, “bạn ơi” is a neutral choice for people about your age.

sections.heading: Call, don’t point
sections.text: Avoid pointing at people, or patting them on the back or head.

stories.appliesTo: Shops, cafés and streets in Hà Nội. Word meanings come from Vietnamese dictionaries; how people use them, from linguists who recorded conversations in Hà Nội and from the national tourism authority.
stories.varies: Which family word fits depends on how old the other person seems to you, and people judge that differently. The south uses dạ where the north often says vâng.

paras.text: In a Hà Nội café people rarely say “excuse me” to get attention. A customer calls *em ơi!* to a young waiter, or *chị ơi!* to a woman a little older behind the counter. That small word, [[oi|ơi]], is how people get each other’s attention in Hà Nội, and the word in front of it says who they think they are talking to.

It is one of the most useful things a visitor can learn, and one of the easiest. This guide covers calling, asking and answering politely, and the gestures that go with them. For the family words themselves in depth, see [why people use family words with strangers](story:st-family-words).

items.text: Family word + ơi: chị ơi, anh ơi, em ơi.
Bạn ơi, for someone about your age.
Add ạ to be polite.

paras.text: Choose the family word that fits how old the person looks to you: *em* for someone younger, *chị* or *anh* for a woman or man a bit older, *cô* or *chú* for someone your aunt’s or uncle’s age, *bà* or *ông* for someone your grandparents’ age. The national tourism authority suggests *bạn ơi*, hey friend, when you are not sure; it suits people of about your own age.
Add *ơi* and say it clearly: *chị ơi!* It is friendly, not rude; it is the same word a child uses to call *mẹ ơi*, Mum. Use your voice rather than your hand.
Then ask, and end with *ạ*, a small particle of respect or warmth: *Hồ Hoàn Kiếm ở đâu ạ?*, Where is Hoàn Kiếm Lake, please? It works after a greeting too: a pupil says *Em chào thầy ạ* to a teacher.

If someone calls you, the polite reply is *dạ*. Answering *ơi* is fine only to an equal or someone younger. For yes, say *vâng*, or *vâng ạ* to be warmer. An old saying sums it up: *gọi dạ, bảo vâng*, answer a call with dạ, an instruction with vâng.
When you pay or pass something, use both hands, or at least your right hand, especially with someone older.

Linguists who recorded about 35 hours of conversation in Hà Nội cafés and restaurants found that family words were the default way to refer to the person spoken to. They are never used both ways round: if you call someone *em*, they call you *anh* or *chị*. And seniority is not mechanical. People born in the same year may treat each other as equals; five years’ difference matters to some pairs and not to others.

The other person may decide for you. A British writer living in Hà Nội was greeted by a bakery owner with *chào anh*, and answered *chào em*. She told him he could not call her *em*: she had set the terms, whatever their real ages. People guess age from looks and circumstances, he wrote; his wife’s advice when unsure was simply to say *chào bác*.

paras.text: Family words are the language of buying and selling. In a study of 500 market conversations in Hà Nội, Huế, Nha Trang and Hồ Chí Minh City, 80 percent of questions used them, partly because they make buyer and seller sound close. An old rule of address explains the choice: *xưng khiêm, hô tôn*, speak of yourself modestly and of the other person respectfully.
In practice: *chị ơi* or *anh ơi* for staff who look older than you, *em ơi* for those who look younger, and *ạ* on the end of your question.

Textbooks teach *tôi*, I, and *bạn*, you, because they are the most neutral pair. In everyday talk they sound formal or distant, the language of first meetings. Between two middle-aged neighbours, *tôi* and *bạn* would sound odd; *chị* and *em* would be natural. Among friends in the north the casual pair is *tớ* and *cậu*.

paras.text: Calling with *ơi* does the job that a pointed finger or a wave might do elsewhere. Pointing at people with the index finger is seen as disrespectful, and beckoning with one finger, palm up, as offensive. Avoid patting people on the back or the head, particularly anyone older than you; touching someone’s head, or passing something over it, is seen as offensive.
If you must wave someone over, many people advise keeping the palm down and moving the fingers towards you. Better still, call.

Others answered that no rule says so, and linguists note that no official standard of pronunciation has been fixed. What a visitor hears in Hà Nội is the north’s *vâng* and *ạ*, alongside the *dạ* that every region shares.

stories.title: Why does the host keep filling your bowl?
stories.dek: Hospitality you can see: a full bowl, a full glass, a bill already paid. What hosts do, what the etiquette books say, and how to say “enough” kindly.

sections.text: Serving a guest, topping up drinks and choosing the best pieces for their bowl, is one way hosts show hospitality.

sections.heading: Saying you have had enough
sections.text: To decline more food, politely say that you are very full.

sections.heading: When you eat out
sections.text: The person who invited usually pays; otherwise it is often the most senior person.

stories.appliesTo: Meals as a guest at home and in restaurants in Hà Nội, from the national tourism authority, the foreign ministry’s newspaper, Vietnamese press and the law.
stories.varies: Families, generations and occasions differ: a family dinner is not a business banquet. Laws and fines are as of 2026.

paras.text: You have barely finished a mouthful when a piece of fish lands in your bowl. You eat it; a piece of pork follows. Your glass is never empty for long. For a guest at a Vietnamese table this can feel like a lot, and it is meant to: serving a guest, choosing the best pieces for them and keeping their glass full is how a host shows care.

Not everyone agrees on how far this should go. The national tourism authority describes it as normal hospitality; a protocol column in the foreign ministry’s newspaper advises hosts to hold back. This story compares the two, and explains how to say “enough”, to food, to drink and to the bill, without giving offence.

items.text: A sign of care. Eat what you can.
Say you are very full: *no rồi*.
Pressing someone to drink is illegal since 2020.
Usually paid by whoever invited.

blocks.heading: Two views of a full bowl

paras.text: At a family table, the host putting food in your bowl is the custom the tourism authority describes, and the one most visitors meet. It says, more clearly than words, that you are welcome and that the best of the meal is for you.

The foreign ministry’s newspaper, *Thế giới & Việt Nam*, sets out a stricter etiquette. Never serve someone with the chopsticks you eat with: turn them round or use serving chopsticks. Do not press food on a guest. At a formal banquet, offer in words, *mời anh lấy thêm*, “please, have some more”, and let guests serve themselves. A guest who would rather do so can say so, gently: *cứ để tôi tự nhiên*, “let me help myself”.

paras.text: The kind way to stop is to say that you are very full, *no rồi*, and to say it more than once. A first refusal can sound like politeness; the second and third are believed. Leave a little in your bowl if you really cannot eat more; an empty bowl may simply be refilled.
Praise the food as you go. A host may call the meal simple, just rice and greens; that is modesty, and it is your cue to say how good it is.

Drinking together is a big part of hospitality, and pressure is real. A foreign resident writing in VnExpress described tables shouting *trăm phần trăm*, empty your glass, and guests treated as impolite for refusing. Expats interviewed in 2025 said the hardest words to escape were “just one drink”. A cultural researcher traces the custom to village ritual and calls today’s drinking excessive.

The law has changed the balance. The 2019 alcohol law, in force since 2020, bans urging, coaxing or forcing anyone to drink; under Decree 117/2020, forcing someone can cost 1–3 million đồng. A health ministry official said the point is to change behaviour, not to fine people, and that the pressure comes mostly from bosses, older relatives and fathers.

Driving is the strongest reason of all. Vietnam allows no alcohol at all for anyone at the wheel or on a motorbike, and since 2025 the fines have been heavy: 2–10 million đồng for a motorbike rider and 6–40 million đồng for a car driver, with the licence suspended for up to two years at the highest level.
Tell your host before the first round that you are not drinking alcohol. It is easier than refusing a glass already poured.
Health, religion or “I am driving” are understood. With zero tolerance for drivers, the last one is hard to argue with.
Fill your glass with tea, water or a soft drink and raise it with everyone. The toast is about being together, not about the drink.
If someone insists, smile, thank them and talk about something else.

paras.text: When you eat out, the person who made the invitation usually pays. If nobody clearly invited, the most senior person often does. If you are invited, let your host pay, thank them, and offer to treat them next time.

Among friends paying can turn into a contest, with people racing to the till or one friend quietly settling the bill before the others notice. A 2026 Tiền Phong essay noted that many young people now prefer to split the bill and each pay their own share.

stories.title: A table of shared dishes
stories.dek: Rice in your bowl, everything else in the middle. How a Hà Nội family meal is laid out, who sits where, who starts, and what happens when the glasses come out.

sections.text: Meals are shared: dishes in the middle, a small rice bowl and chopsticks each.

sections.heading: Passing things
sections.text: Pass dishes with both hands or the right hand. Hold the soup spoon in the left.

sections.heading: Raising a glass
sections.text: People toast together with “dô”, “zo” in the North and “yo” in the South.
You can join a toast with any drink.

stories.appliesTo: Family meals at home in Hà Nội and northern Vietnam, from the national tourism authority’s etiquette guide and Vietnamese press.
stories.varies: Many families now eat at a table and keep fewer of the old customs; city and village, young and old, do things differently.

paras.text: At a Vietnamese family meal nobody has a plate of their own. The food sits in the middle, often on a round [[mam|mâm]], a tray, and everyone has a small bowl of rice and a pair of chopsticks. You take a little from the shared dishes, put it on your rice, eat, and take a little more. The national tourism authority puts it simply: mealtimes are about sharing.

That one idea shapes everything else: where people sit, who starts, how you reach for food, even how you raise a glass. Researchers who study the family meal describe it as a mix of food and conversation, a daily rehearsal of who is who in the family. You do not need to know every rule to be a good guest. It helps to know what is going on around you.

items.text: A small rice bowl, chopsticks, maybe a spoon.
Every other dish, in the middle.
When the oldest person starts.
“Một, hai, ba, dô!”, with any drink.

paras.text: A traditional tray is laid out around a small bowl of fish sauce or dipping sauce in the centre. Around it go a vegetable, a dish of meat or fish, and a soup. For generations families sat cross-legged on a mat around the tray; many now eat at a table, but the layout is the same.

What goes on it is everyday food. VnExpress described a typical northern summer meal: boiled pork belly, a crab soup cooked with jute leaves and gourd, fried tofu dipped in shrimp paste, boiled morning glory, salted baby aubergines, and fruit to finish. Nothing is served in courses. It all arrives together, and you move between the dishes as you like.

blocks.heading: The person by the rice pot

paras.text: In an old Hà Nội family, the rice pot sat on the floor beside the tray, and one person sat at the head of it. That was usually the grandmother, the mother or the eldest daughter-in-law, and an essay on Hà Nội food calls her the most important woman in the house. When your bowl was empty she refilled it, so that nobody had to get up during the meal.
A guest at a family table today will often see the same thing in a smaller form: someone, usually the host, keeps an eye on everyone’s bowl. Hold yours out when it is offered, and say thank you.

blocks.heading: Who sits where, and who starts

paras.text: Seats follow age. A northern proverb says *ăn trông nồi, ngồi trông hướng*: watch the pot as you eat, watch where you sit. The best places go to the grandparents and parents. At village feasts the most senior guests may have a tray of their own, set a little apart.

Before anyone eats, the younger people invite their elders, one by one: *Con mời bà ăn cơm*, “I invite you to eat, grandmother”. In older Hà Nội speech it was *mời mẹ xơi cơm ạ*, with the polite verb *xơi*. Nobody starts until the oldest person picks up their bowl. At the end, the younger ones ask leave to get up, and bring the elders tea.

This custom is fading. A 2025 VnExpress report found many families have dropped the invitation altogether, as busy households eat together less often. As a guest, a simple [[moi|mời]] to the people around you before you start is always welcome, and never wrong.

paras.text: Pass dishes with both hands or with the right hand, not the left. If there is soup, the spoon goes in your left hand while the chopsticks stay in your right. Soup from the shared bowl is ladled into your own bowl; you never sip from the serving spoon.

Take from the side of the dish nearest you, and do not dig around for the best piece. When you take from a shared dish, or put food in someone else’s bowl, many families turn their chopsticks round and use the other end, or use a pair of serving chopsticks. Our guide to [chopsticks](story:st-chop) has the details.

Here the sources disagree, and so do Vietnamese families. The traditional custom is to leave one piece on a shared dish, a polite last piece, so that nobody looks greedy. A proverb jokes about it: eat it all and get a beating, leave some and lose a wife.

Times have changed. When VnExpress asked readers, many said that leaving food is wasteful, and that clearing your bowl is how you show respect for the cook. The safest course is the one the host sets: if they urge you to take the last piece, take it.

blocks.text: Watch the pot as you eat, watch where you sit.
blocks.by: Northern proverb, ăn trông nồi, ngồi trông hướng

paras.text: When there are drinks, nobody drinks alone. People raise their glasses together, often counting *một, hai, ba, dô!*, one, two, three, cheers, and drink as a group. *Dô* is said “zo” in the North and “yo” in the South. Someone may call out *trăm phần trăm*, “one hundred per cent”: empty the glass.

Toasts follow rank too. VnExpress told the story of a new son-in-law scolded for raising his glass to the head of his wife’s clan: only the elder’s equals, like his father-in-law, should have invited him to drink. As a guest you will not be expected to know this; wait to be toasted, and toast back.

You can join any toast with any drink. Whether you drink alcohol is your choice, and the law is on your side: since 2020 it has been illegal to urge or force anyone to drink. Our story on [hosts and guests](story:st-host) covers saying no.

Outside the home, Hà Nội drinks [[bia-hoi|bia hơi]]: fresh, unpasteurised beer, brewed to be drunk within a day or so and poured at pavement corners into thick glasses. In the subsidy era it arrived in 100-litre aluminium tanks; since 2000 the city’s brewer has delivered it in 50-litre kegs. The first foamy cups from a new keg have a nickname, *bia cắt tiết*.

It is part of why Vietnam drinks a lot of beer: by one brewer’s estimate about 4.6 billion litres in 2024, the eighth-largest total in the world. From 2026 the tax on beer rises every year, to 90% by 2031.

stories.dek: Which end to use, where to rest them, and why they should never stand in your rice. A short guide to the two things you hold all through a meal.

sections.text: Chopsticks standing upright in rice look like the incense and rice offered to the dead, so they are rested across the bowl or on the table instead.

sections.text: To serve someone, turn your chopsticks round or use serving chopsticks.

stories.varies: Families differ, and street stalls are more relaxed than a family table. The luck beliefs are beliefs, held by some people more than others.

paras.text: At a Vietnamese meal you hold two things from start to finish: a small bowl of rice and a pair of chopsticks. The dishes are shared, so the chopsticks do more than carry food to your mouth. They reach into the middle of the table, into other people’s bowls, and they rest beside you when you stop. That is why people notice how you use them.

Most of what follows is ordinary politeness, the kind any family would teach a child. A few customs come from beliefs about the dead and about luck. Some are shared across East Asia; a widely read VnExpress list of chopstick taboos was adapted from a Chinese source. None of it needs to make you nervous: hosts forgive a visitor almost anything, and watching the people around you is the best guide.

blocks.heading: Through a meal, step by step

paras.text: Wait for the oldest person to pick up their bowl. In many northern families the younger people first invite each elder to eat. A quiet *mời* to the people beside you is always welcome.

items.title: Taking from the shared dishes

paras.text: Take a little at a time, from the side of the dish nearest you, and put it on your rice. Do not dig through the dish for the best piece.

Many families keep a pair of serving chopsticks, or turn their own round and use the clean end for the shared dishes. One VnExpress reader wrote that her family always kept shared chopsticks and spoons, and that if you are not sure, you can simply ask.

items.caption: Shared dishes round a bowl of dipping sauce.

paras.text: Hosts often put food in a guest’s bowl, and you may want to do the same for an elder. Never do it with the end you eat from: turn your chopsticks round, or use the serving pair. The foreign ministry’s newspaper says the same.
Ladle soup from the shared bowl into your own; never sip from the serving spoon. The spoon goes in your left hand, the chopsticks stay in your right.

When you pause, lay your chopsticks across the top of your bowl or on the table beside it. Never leave them standing upright in the rice: it recalls the incense sticks and the bowl of rice offered to the dead at an altar.
Lay the chopsticks down neatly. In traditional families the younger people ask leave before getting up, and bring the elders tea.

On a family altar, a bowl of rice is offered to the ancestors and sticks of incense are planted upright in a bowl of sand or rice. Chopsticks standing in a bowl of rice look the same. At a meal for the living, that is a picture nobody wants to see. The Cultural Atlas, the national broadcaster’s foreign service and VnExpress all mention it.

It is a belief, but a widely shared one, in Vietnam and across East Asia, and it is the one chopstick rule a host is most likely to notice. Our story on [arriving at a Hà Nội home](story:st-arrive-home) says more about the family altar.

blocks.text: Some of these customs are shared with China, Korea and Japan. The VnExpress list of chopstick taboos we cite was adapted from a Chinese-language source, so treat it as East Asian etiquette in general.

When someone at the head of the rice pot offers to refill your bowl, hold it out with both hands and say thank you. In old Hà Nội families that person, usually the grandmother or mother, made sure nobody had to get up during the meal.

stories.title: The stelae of doctoral laureates
stories.dek: Eighty-two stones on the backs of stone turtles, carved with the names of 1,304 scholars. Three centuries of royal examinations, and why you may no longer touch them.

sections.text: The stelae record the names of people who passed the highest royal examinations: 82 stelae for exams held from 1442 to 1779.

sections.heading: On UNESCO’s registers
sections.text: They were added to UNESCO’s Memory of the World registers in 2010 and 2011.

sections.heading: Looking, not touching
sections.text: The site asks visitors not to touch, write on or draw on the stelae.

stories.appliesTo: The doctoral stelae at Văn Miếu – Quốc Tử Giám, from UNESCO’s Memory of the World record, the site’s official pages and Vietnamese press.
stories.varies: Specific to this site. Sources differ slightly on the number of names (1,304 or 1,307).

paras.text: In the third courtyard of Văn Miếu, on either side of a square pond, stand two rows of stone turtles. Each carries a stone slab on its back, and each slab is carved with the names of the men who passed one royal examination: when it was held, who set it, who came first, and where each laureate came from. There are 82 of them, for exams held between 1442 and 1779, and together they name 1,304 doctors.
They are the closest thing Vietnam has to a stone archive of its scholars. UNESCO added them to its Memory of the World register in 2011, and Vietnam made them a national treasure in 2015.

items.text: 82 stelae, 82 examinations.

paras.text: To earn a place on a stele, a scholar had to pass three examinations: the regional *thi Hương*, the metropolitan *thi Hội* in the capital, and the palace *thi Đình*, where candidates knelt in the courtyard before the king to receive the question. From 1434 the exams were held every three years, and from 1442 those who passed the last stage were titled [[tien-si|tiến sĩ]].

The stelae begin with that year. In 1484 King Lê Thánh Tông ordered a stele for the examination of 1442, held 42 years before. Its text, written by the scholar Thân Nhân Trung, contains a famous line: *hiền tài là nguyên khí quốc gia*, talented people are the vital force of the nation.

items.text: After years of rubbing for luck, a steel fence replaces the ropes.
items.caption: A row of stelae behind the fence.

items.title: National treasure
items.text: The 82 stelae are named a national treasure.

paras.text: Each stele stands on a stone turtle, the tallest more than two metres high. UNESCO’s record describes the turtles but does not explain them. The folklorist Ngô Đức Thịnh does: the turtle lives long and is the very picture of endurance, so a stele on its back means the laureates’ names will be kept from generation to generation, for ever.
Turtles appear elsewhere in Hà Nội’s stories too, above all in the legend of [the returned sword](story:st-sword-lake) at Hoàn Kiếm Lake.

blocks.heading: Rubbing for luck, and the fence

paras.text: For generations students rubbed the turtles’ heads before their exams, hoping some of the laureates’ luck would pass to them. By 2010 UNESCO’s nomination noted that touching and rubbing was wearing the stones down. In 2012 the rows were roped off and student volunteers stood guard in exam season; in 2014 a steel fence went up.
The rule today is simple: look, do not touch. The site’s rules forbid touching, writing or drawing on the stelae and buildings.

The stones also record politics. Some of their texts praised the Trịnh lords, and later rulers did not want that remembered: after an order of 1840 under the Nguyễn, those lines were chiselled off some of the stelae.

Nor did the stones go up as the exams were held. They came in batches: the first under Lê Thánh Tông, then 25 in 1653, 21 in 1717 and 22 between 1721 and 1780, often recording examinations held many years earlier, just as the first stele did for 1442.

What survived is still remarkable: 82 stones covering 82 examinations over more than three centuries, with each laureate’s name, home village and position. UNESCO added them to its Memory of the World register for Asia and the Pacific in 2010, and to the international register in 2011.

stories.title: Visiting a temple or pagoda
stories.dek: What to wear, how many incense sticks, where the money goes, and when to put the camera away. A practical guide to Hà Nội’s places of worship, from the rules sites publish to the customs they leave unsaid.

sections.heading: The site’s own rules
sections.text: Văn Miếu – Quốc Tử Giám asks visitors to dress respectfully, keep quiet and not touch the stelae or buildings.

sections.heading: General guidance
sections.text: Dress modestly and take off hats.

stories.appliesTo: Pagodas, temples and heritage sites in Hà Nội. Site rules come from the sites themselves; general guidance from the national tourism authority.
stories.varies: Each site has its own rules, and they change. Check signs on the day.

paras.text: At Hà Nội’s pagodas and temples a few things matter: what you wear, where you put your feet and your money, and when you lift your camera. This guide sets out what the sites themselves ask, what general guidance adds, and where both are silent.

items.text: Shoulders and knees covered; hat off.
Usually one or three sticks.
In the donation box, not on statues.
Ask before photographing people.

paras.text: General guidance for temples in Vietnam is to dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees, and to take off your hat. Văn Miếu’s own rules ask for respectful dress in its places of worship. If you are touring in shorts, a scarf or light trousers in your bag solves it.
The national tourism authority advises taking off shoes at temples; you may carry them, just not wear them.

Custom favours an odd number of sticks, usually three or one. The abbot of the One Pillar pagoda, asked about it, said one, two or three are all fine, and that pagodas set no rule; what matters is sincerity.

On the first day of Tết 2025, reporters found the trays at Phủ Tây Hồ and Trấn Quốc held only fruit and sweets, with no votive paper and no meat. Many temples now limit paper offerings; see [paper offerings](story:st-paper-offerings).

For years visitors tucked small notes into statues’ hands and piled them at their feet. The rules now ask festival organisers to guide people to put money only in the places set aside, and money-changing for a fee inside sites is to stop. Use the donation box.
Keep your voice down in the halls. At heritage sites such as Văn Miếu you must not touch, write on or draw on stelae, statues or buildings.

Ask before photographing people, especially anyone praying. Do not use flash where signs ask for no photos, and avoid posing for selfies with Buddha statues, which can be seen as disrespectful. Where the published rules are silent, as Văn Miếu’s are, look for signs or ask staff.

paras.text: The 1st and 15th of each lunar month are the days families light incense, at home and at temples, and the first days of the year are the busiest of all: on the first day of Tết 2025 crowds were at Phủ Tây Hồ from nine in the morning. If you want a quiet visit, avoid those days; if you want to see the city at worship, go then.

On the busiest days the halls may be closed to the crowd. At Phủ Tây Hồ on the first day of Tết 2025, visitors made their offerings from the courtyard rather than inside. Follow the staff and the signs, and give the people praying room.

Many shops and homes keep a small altar on the floor near the door, for the god of wealth and the earth god. The national tourism authority advises not stepping over it or walking directly in front of it. Our story on [the family altar](story:st-family-altar) explains it.

Heritage sites charge for entry. Văn Miếu opens every day from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and a ticket is 70,000 đồng, half price for students and people over 60. The Imperial Citadel is open 8:00–17:00 and costs 100,000 đồng.

Some customs have had to change. For years students rubbed the heads of the stone turtles under Văn Miếu’s stelae for luck before their exams, until the wear forced the site to fence them off in 2014. Look, and leave them be.

blocks.heading: Paper offerings and the new rules

paras.text: Hà Nội’s temples have tightened up on paper offerings. In the 2026 festival season Quán Thánh asked visitors not to bring paper offerings into the main shrine, Kim Liên did not allow burning in its main worship area, and Phủ Tây Hồ set up a supervised place for burning. The city also forbids scattering rice or salt and sticking incense into trees. If you buy offerings at the gate, ask what the temple allows.

On the first day of the year many Hanoians go to pagodas and temples such as Trấn Quốc and Ngọc Sơn to pray for peace, and calligraphers write characters for the new year at Ngọc Sơn and Văn Miếu. In spring pilgrims travel by boat to the Hương pagoda; in 2026 the festival ran from February to May and 135,900 people came in its first five days.
For the difference between a chùa, a đền and a đình, and what each one honours, see [Chùa, đền, đình](story:st-sacred-places).

stories.title: Arriving at a family home
stories.dek: Shoes at the door, the eldest first, a pot of tea and a host who keeps filling your bowl: how a visit to a Hà Nội home usually goes.

sections.text: Shoes are usually taken off at the door of a home.

sections.heading: Who to greet first
sections.text: Greet the oldest people first, and smile at everyone.

sections.heading: Being looked after
sections.text: Hosts serve their guests, refill their drinks and put the best pieces in their bowl.

stories.appliesTo: Visiting a family at home in Hà Nội and northern Vietnam. Most of what follows holds across the country.
stories.varies: Families differ, and so do generations and regions. Follow how your host introduces themself and what they do; gift taboos are beliefs, not rules.

paras.text: Being invited home is a step up from being taken to a restaurant. In Hà Nội, where families often share narrow tube houses or high-rise flats, the invitation means being let into the place where the generations meet and the ancestors are remembered. What follows is how a visit usually goes, step by step.

None of it is a test. Hosts expect a foreign guest to get things slightly wrong, and the easiest rule is to watch them: where the shoes go, who sits where, who starts eating. When you are not sure, ask.

Don’t arrive empty-handed. Fruit is the usual gift; biscuits or a cake, flowers or soft drinks work too, and something from your own country is a good talking point. Hand it over with both hands and play it down: it is just a small thing. Your host may put it aside without opening it, and may well send you home with fruit of their own.
Take your shoes off just outside the door, next to the family’s own.

Greet people in order of age, starting with the grandparents. Stand, nod or bow slightly from the shoulders, and let an older person offer a hand first. Use a family word: *Cháu chào bác* to someone older than your parents, *cô* or *chú* to someone younger than them, *ông* or *bà* to a grandparent. Adding *ạ* at the end sounds respectful. Don’t be surprised if someone asks how old you are; it is how they work out what to call you.
Older Hà Nội families once expected visiting children to fold their arms when they greeted the parents. You will rarely see it now, but it shows how much the greeting matters.

items.title: Tea first

paras.text: Before anything else, there is usually tea. The host brews a fresh pot and pours small cups; a saying has it that a cup of tea opens the conversation. Take the cup with both hands, sip, and let the talk begin. You may be asked whether you have eaten, *ăn cơm chưa?*, which is a greeting and, near a mealtime, often an invitation to stay.

items.caption: A teapot and cups set out for guests.

items.title: At the table

paras.text: Wait to be shown where to sit, and wait to start. In many northern families the younger members invite each elder to eat in turn, and nobody begins until the oldest person does. Your host will probably put food in your bowl, again and again. Eat what you can; to stop, say you are full, kindly and more than once, and leave the last piece on a shared dish unless you are urged to take it.
Your host may call it a simple meal of rice and greens. Say how good it is. And never leave your chopsticks standing upright in the rice: it recalls the incense sticks offered to the dead.

items.caption: A family meal: fish, greens, vegetables and small bowls of dipping sauce.

paras.text: There is no set ritual for leaving. Wait for a natural pause, thank your hosts for looking after you, and say goodbye to the elders as you greeted them. Avoid glancing at the clock or saying you are tired. One warm thank-you means more than many automatic ones.

Somewhere in the house there will be an ancestral altar: photographs or name tablets of the family’s dead, an incense bowl, candles, fruit and flowers. Families rich and poor keep one, and it is the most sacred place in the home. In a traditional house it stands in the centre and at the highest point; in the tall, narrow houses of Hà Nội it is often on the top floor.

As a guest, give it room. Don’t step over an altar on the floor, walk straight in front of it or put your things down before it. People once placed a visitor’s gift on the altar so the ancestors could see it; that custom has mostly faded, but if your host does it, it is a compliment.

paras.text: The picture of three generations under one roof is only partly true now. The 2019 census counted 3.5 people per household across Vietnam and 3.3 in the Red River Delta around Hà Nội. Researchers disagree on how many older people still live with their children: one study found the share fell to 28% by 2017 in two provinces, another national survey put it above 60%. stories.title: Why raise your hand to cross?
stories.dek: Nearly seven million motorbikes, few traffic lights in the old streets, and a law that asks pedestrians to signal with a hand. How Hà Nội crosses the road.

sections.text: Vietnam’s road law asks pedestrians to cross at lights, marked crossings, bridges or tunnels where there are any.

sections.heading: Where there is no crossing
sections.text: Watch the traffic, cross when it is safe and give a hand signal. Crossing without one can be fined.

sections.heading: Keep watching anyway
sections.text: Compliance with road rules is poor, so stay alert and keep your bag away from the traffic.

sections.heading: A steady pace
sections.text: Walk steadily so riders can predict you, or cross with local people.

stories.appliesTo: Crossing streets in Hà Nội and other Vietnamese cities. The law applies nationwide.
stories.varies: Traffic differs from street to street and hour to hour, and rules for the city centre are changing. This is not legal advice.

paras.text: The first time you stand at the edge of a Hà Nội street, it can look like a river with no bridge. Motorbikes pour past in both directions, weaving, hooting, filling every gap. There is a reason the city feels like this: it has about 6.9 million motorbikes and 1.1 million cars, and more than 450,000 motorbikes inside the inner ring road alone.

People cross anyway, all day, and so can you. Vietnam’s road law even tells you how, down to a detail that surprises visitors: where there is no crossing, raise your hand. This guide explains the rule, the fine, and the local habits that matter as much as either.

items.text: At lights, marked crossings, footbridges or underpasses, if there are any.
Watch the traffic, cross when it is safe, and signal with your hand.
No hand signal needed; follow the lights.
150,000–250,000 đồng for crossing in the wrong place or without the signal where it is required.

items.title: Look for a crossing first

paras.text: The law, in force since January 2025, says to cross at traffic lights, a marked crossing, a footbridge or an underpass where one exists, and to follow the signals. On a marked crossing you do not need to raise your hand.

items.caption: Traffic lights at an Old Quarter junction.

items.title: Wait for a gap, not an empty road

paras.text: An empty road may never come. Watch the oncoming traffic and choose a moment when it thins. If you are unsure, stand beside local people who are about to cross and move when they do.
Let cars, buses and lorries pass first. A motorbike can steer around you; a bus cannot.

Where there is no crossing, the law asks you to give a hand signal while you cross. It does not say how; the point is that riders can see you mean to cross. Crossing without the signal where it is required, or in a place you should not, can be fined 150,000–250,000 đồng, more than double the old fine.

items.title: Walk steadily. Don’t stop, don’t run

paras.text: This is the part locals stress most. Walk at an even pace, in a straight line, and look at the riders coming towards you. They judge where you will be and steer around you. Stopping halfway, stepping back or suddenly running is what confuses them.

items.title: Keep watching, and keep your bag close

paras.text: The UK government’s travel advice is blunt: compliance with road laws is poor, so stay aware of motorbikes the whole way across. Thieves on motorbikes snatch bags, so carry yours in front of you or on the side away from the road.

Hà Nội’s own writers are frank about it. One reader of VnExpress stood at a busy junction and counted 37 people crossing during a single red light; only four used the zebra crossing. Pavements are often blocked by parked bikes and stalls, and at some wide junctions the green light lasts barely long enough to cross. A columnist in Việt Nam News put it simply: don’t expect a vehicle to stop for you.

Their advice is the same as a motorbike-taxi driver’s: walk evenly, look straight ahead, don’t stop, don’t run, don’t hesitate. It works because riders read a steady walker easily. It is local know-how rather than a rule, and it works far better with motorbikes than with cars.

blocks.caption: Motorbikes turning through an Old Quarter junction.

paras.text: Traffic is a real risk in Vietnam, but the numbers are falling. Police counted 10,379 road deaths across the country in the year to mid-December 2025, about 6% fewer than the year before, and 7,198 in the first nine months of 2026. The World Health Organization’s estimates, made a different way and running higher, show the death rate falling from 25.4 per 100,000 people in 2010 to 17.7 in 2021.

blocks.text: Police counts and WHO estimates are measured differently and should not be compared directly. Both point the same way: down.

blocks.heading: A quieter centre on weekend nights

paras.text: Crossing is easiest of all where there is no traffic. Every Friday to Sunday evening, the streets around Hoàn Kiếm Lake close to vehicles and become a walking space. In July 2026 this became the first phase of a low-emission pilot zone. A government directive had asked Hà Nội to keep petrol motorbikes out of the whole inner ring road from that date; the city chose to go in stages, and pushed the wider limits back to 2028.

blocks.caption: The car-free lakeside on a Saturday night.

paras.text: The law asks adults to lead children under seven by the hand when crossing, and asks everyone to help children, pregnant women, older people and disabled people across the road. Use the pavement where there is one, and keep to the right-hand edge of the road where there isn’t.

options.feedback: Stopping suddenly is what riders find hardest to predict. They are already steering for where you were going to be.

options.feedback: A steady walker is easy to read. The rider will pass behind or in front of you.

options.label: Run to the other side

stories.title: Asking before a photo
stories.dek: A vendor’s bicycle, a temple courtyard, a pair of friends in áo dài: Hà Nội is easy to photograph. The people in the picture get a say, and a few places have rules of their own.

sections.text: Ask before photographing people; a calm, friendly request usually works.

sections.heading: At heritage sites
sections.text: Some sites publish no photo rules, so ask staff or look for signs.

stories.appliesTo: Taking photos of people and places in Hà Nội. The laws apply across Vietnam.
stories.varies: Each person decides for themself, and each site may post its own rules. Laws and fines are as reported in 2025–26; this is not legal advice.

paras.text: Hà Nội is easy to photograph: a woman in a conical hat with a bicycle full of flowers, a red bridge over green water, friends in [[aodai|áo dài]] posing in an Old Quarter lane. It is tempting to raise the camera and shoot.

Ask first. The national tourism authority puts it plainly, and adds the good news: most people will be happy to have their picture taken, and asking often starts a conversation. This guide covers how to ask, what the law says, and the few places where the answer is always no.

blocks.heading: Taking a portrait, step by step

paras.text: Catch the person’s eye, smile, lift the camera slightly and tilt your head: the question is clear in any language. If you can, say it: *Tôi chụp ảnh bạn được không?* A nod means yes; a wave of the hand or a turned shoulder means no, and that is the end of it.

items.title: Take your time, then show them

paras.text: Once someone agrees, there is no need to rush. Afterwards, turn the screen round and show them. People often laugh, point, ask for another. If they ask you to delete it, delete it while they watch.

items.caption: A fruit seller with her baskets.

paras.text: Ask a parent before photographing a child, and don’t pat a child on the head to say thank you: touching the top of the head, especially a child’s, is considered rude.

items.title: Agree a price before you pose

paras.text: In the streets around Hoàn Kiếm Lake, a vendor may offer to put her shoulder pole and baskets on you for a photo. It is a long-reported routine, and money is usually expected afterwards; in 2012 the district acted against nearly 140 vendors who did it without asking. If you want the picture, agree a price first. If you don’t, say no with a smile and walk on.

items.caption: A vendor by Hoàn Kiếm Lake.

paras.text: Taking a photo in a public place is one thing; publishing it is another. Under Vietnam’s Civil Code, using someone’s image needs their consent, and using it commercially means paying them unless you agree otherwise. Photos of public events, such as performances and sports, are an exception, as long as the use does not harm the person’s dignity.

blocks.heading: What the law does and does not say

paras.text: Vietnam’s Civil Code of 2015 gives every person rights over their own image. The key word is *use*: the article is about publishing a picture, putting it in an advertisement or selling it, not about pressing the shutter in a public street. Using a person’s image needs their consent; using it to make money means paying them, unless you both agree otherwise.

There are two exceptions. Images used in the national or public interest need no consent, and nor do images taken at public activities such as conferences, sports matches and performances, provided the use does not damage the person’s honour, dignity or reputation. A separate article protects private life: collecting or publishing information about someone’s private life needs their consent. Anyone whose image is misused can ask a court to order it taken down or destroyed and to award compensation.
In practice: a street scene for your own album is fine; a close portrait you post online or sell is where consent matters most.

A temple is a place of worship before it is a sight. Dress modestly, take off your hat and, where asked, your shoes. Look for signs before you photograph inside, and never use flash where they ask for no photos. Many Buddhists find photos of Buddha statues, and especially selfies with them, disrespectful.
People who are praying are not part of the scenery. Ask, or wait until they have finished.

stories.title: Keeping your cool in public
stories.dek: Why a quiet word works better than a raised voice, what a smile can mean, and which gestures to keep in your pocket.

sections.text: Saving face matters: keep calm in public and avoid loud arguments.

sections.heading: Gestures to avoid
sections.text: Don’t point at people or pat them on the head, especially if they are older than you.

stories.appliesTo: Everyday encounters in Hà Nội: shops, taxis, restaurants, offices and the street.
stories.varies: General guidance, not a rule. People, generations and situations differ, and the scholars quoted here warn against treating it as a stereotype.

paras.text: Sooner or later something will go wrong: a wrong order, a taxi that takes the long way, a price that changes at the till. The instinct many visitors bring is to make the problem clear, firmly and loudly. In Hà Nội, that is usually the slowest way to fix it.

The national tourism authority’s advice is short: keep your cool, avoid loud arguments and making a scene, and don’t berate people for mistakes. Behind it is an idea that shapes everyday life here, and has its own small vocabulary: face.

Face stands for a person’s reputation, dignity and honour in the eyes of others. You give someone face by treating them with respect and paying compliments; they lose it when they are criticised or shown up in public. A shop assistant scolded in front of colleagues has lost face. So, in a different way, has the customer who shouted.

Researchers in Vietnam describe face as both personal and shared. It belongs to you, but also to your family and group, and it depends on what others think. One study finds that when someone higher up a hierarchy loses face, an older person, a manager, an official, the consequences are taken more seriously. That is why a public confrontation with an older or senior person can go especially badly.

items.text: Face: your standing in other people’s eyes.
To lose face, literally “lose the face”.
Honour, of a person or a family.
Pride; *sĩ diện hão* is hollow pride, keeping up appearances.
Modest, playing yourself down.

blocks.text: Vietnamese scholars themselves use these words loosely, often interchangeably, and Vietnamese writers have long criticised *sĩ diện hão*, pride for show. Face is a value people argue about, not a rule they all obey.

paras.text: Age shapes almost every encounter. Vietnam’s tourism authority sums up the attitude in three words, older is wiser, and names the virtue that goes with it: *lễ phép*, being courteous, respectful and even compliant towards older people. The language builds it in, with different words for “you” depending on whether the other person is older or younger, and people will often ask your age soon after meeting so they know which to use.

This is why the same complaint lands differently depending on who receives it. Research on face finds that when someone higher in a hierarchy loses face, the damage is taken more seriously than when someone lower down does. Contradicting an older shopkeeper in front of her family, or a senior official in front of his staff, costs more than the same words said to a teenager behind a counter. If you need to disagree with someone older, do it privately, gently, and with their title: *bác*, *cô*, *chú*.

Everyday speech tends to be indirect and polite. Someone may avoid a flat “no” and say “maybe”, “it’s difficult” or nothing at all; a “yes” may simply mean “I hear you”. A pause before answering is a sign of respect, not hesitation. If you need a clear answer, ask an open question, “what would be possible?”, rather than one that forces a refusal.

Modesty works the same way. People play down their feelings, their cooking and their gifts. A host may even pretend to scold a friend for bringing a present: “why did you go to all that trouble?” A Vietnamese guest hears warmth; a visitor may hear a complaint. None of this means people are dishonest. Observers often note the opposite.

blocks.text: Modesty does not preclude honesty.
blocks.by: The Cultural Atlas, on Vietnamese culture

paras.text: Shouting is generally seen as improper, uncivilised even. It is also, honestly, common: you will hear raised voices in markets, in traffic and across the street. The difference is who is shouting at whom. A visitor raising their voice at a waiter or driver puts the other person in a corner where giving way means losing face.

A smile can mean more than happiness. People may smile or laugh softly when they are embarrassed, apologising, frustrated or nervous, as if to spare you the discomfort. Others keep a serious face that is not unfriendly at all. And from you, a smile goes a long way, especially when you have no shared language.

paras.text: Say the bill is wrong. Lower your voice rather than raising it. Use a polite form of address, *anh ơi*, *chị ơi*, and smile. Describe the problem as a misunderstanding, not an accusation: “I think there may be a mistake here.” Give the other person room to put it right without being shown up. If it is not resolved, ask quietly for a manager, away from the crowd.
It will not always work, and you are not obliged to accept being cheated. But the calm route is usually faster, and it leaves both of you able to walk away with your face intact.

stories.title: Eating at a street-food stall
stories.dek: Order at the front, sit where there is room, eat first and pay on the way out. A guide to Hà Nội’s plastic-stool kitchens: what to order, when, and how to choose one.

sections.text: At a small street-food stall there is often no menu. Order at the front, then choose your own stool; pointing is fine.

sections.heading: Sharing a table
sections.text: At busy times other diners may sit at your table; that is normal.

sections.heading: What is already on the table
sections.text: Herbs come free with noodle dishes, trà đá replaces water, and wiping your chopsticks is normal.

sections.heading: Paying
sections.text: Eat first and pay on the way out. Tipping is not expected.

stories.appliesTo: Small pavement and shopfront stalls in Hà Nội, from the national tourism authority’s street-food guides, Vietnamese press and official pages. Prices from 2026.
stories.varies: Restaurants and cafés work differently, and stalls in other cities have their own habits. Pavement rules in Hà Nội were changing in 2025–26.

paras.text: Much of the best food in Hà Nội is cooked in a space the size of a parked car. A pot of broth on a gas ring, a tray of herbs, a stack of bowls, and a cluster of low plastic stools: that is a restaurant. Many stalls serve only two or three dishes, perfected over years, and some have no sign at all.

The city is proud of them. In 2025 Time Out ranked Hà Nội the second-best street-food city in Asia, and the Michelin Guide now lists stalls alongside restaurants, its director praising the street stalls and family eateries that keep old recipes alive. This guide explains how a stall works, what to eat and when, and how to choose a good one.

items.text: At the front, then sit anywhere.
Trà đá, iced tea, instead of water.
On the way out. Say “tính tiền”.

blocks.heading: A meal at a stall, step by step

items.title: Choose a busy one

paras.text: The national tourism authority’s rule of thumb: the busier the stall, the more likely it is worth the wait. Locals know which cook is good. The health ministry adds a few signs to look for: a clean cooking area, staff wearing gloves, and oil that is not dark from reuse. Avoid stalls that are dusty, smoky or right on the edge of heavy traffic.

items.caption: Plastic stools stacked outside a Hà Nội eatery.

paras.text: Go to the cook, usually at the front by the pot, and order before you sit. If there is no menu, point at what you want and ask for *một suất*, one serving, or *một cái này*, one of these. Or order what the next table is eating.
Pick your own stool or table. At busy times strangers will sit at yours; that is normal, and a smile is enough.

items.title: Use what is on the table

paras.text: Noodle dishes come with a free plate of herbs and greens. On the table you will find a jar of garlic and chilli in vinegar, fish sauce, chilli and lime: vinegar usually goes with beef phở, lime with chicken. Wiping your chopsticks and spoon with a napkin before you eat is normal, and the used napkins, lime husks and herb stalks go in the bin under the table.
Instead of water you will be offered [[tra-da|trà đá]], iced green tea, or hot tea in cold weather.
When you have finished, say *tính tiền* and pay the cook on your way out; someone may add up the bill at your table. Tipping is not expected at stalls.
Carry small notes. Stalls rarely take cards, and a large note can leave the cook without change.

blocks.heading: Hà Nội eats by the clock

paras.text: Stalls keep hours, and so do dishes. Morning stalls open soon after sunrise; lunch is from about half past eleven to one; dinner is busiest from six to eight. Arrive late and the pot may be empty.

Breakfast is the big meal of the street. [Phở](story:st-pho) is the best known, but there is also *bánh cuốn*, delicate steamed rice sheets; *xôi*, sticky rice with savoury toppings; and *bún thang*, a clear noodle soup with many fine toppings that, the tourism authority says, began as a way to use up leftover Tết food. [Bún chả](story:st-bun-cha) belongs to lunch.

paras.text: Street food is regulated. The 2010 Food Safety Law has its own section on it: food must be displayed on clean tables, shelves or stands, with clean ingredients and utensils. Since January 2025 Hà Nội can fine violations up to 6 million đồng, and a revised law with new street-food rules went before the National Assembly in October 2026.

Enforcement is a big job. A city council survey in 2025 counted 6,890 street-food businesses in Hà Nội, out of about 80,000 food businesses of all kinds; since 2021 inspectors had found violations in about one check in seven. We could not find reliable figures for food poisoning from Hà Nội street food, so we do not give any.
The practical advice is the same as in step one: choose busy stalls, food cooked hot in front of you, a clean cooking area, and clean oil.

blocks.text: We could not find Hà Nội food-poisoning figures for 2024–26 from a reliable source, so we have not given any.

paras.text: The stalls are changing. In 2025–26 Hà Nội’s campaign to clear the pavements, described in our story on [life on the pavement](story:st-pavement), pushed many food sellers indoors. One crab-noodle seller on Hàng Cháo moved into an alley a metre wide and lost about two-thirds of the stall’s trade; a xôi seller on Hàng Khoai moved into a shop two hundred metres away and paid double the rent.
Some streets are made for eating. Tống Duy Tân has been the city’s food street since 2000, and in January 2025 it reopened with stone paving, lanterns and a bronze statue of a phở seller.

stories.title: Shopping at a market
stories.dek: A covered market from 1889, a wholesale market that wakes at midnight and a pavement market at the end of every alley. Many prices are talked about, not printed.

sections.text: Đồng Xuân Market, created in 1889, is Hà Nội’s best-known market: three floors of fabric, clothing and household goods.

sections.heading: Asking the price
sections.text: Bargaining is common at stalls where goods have no printed price.

sections.text: It goes best when it is friendly and polite; once you have agreed a price, pay it.

paras.text: Inside Đồng Xuân, more than two thousand stalls are packed under one roof: buttons and bolts of silk, rice cookers, sweets by the kilo. Much of it is sold wholesale to shops across the north.

steps.label: Long Biên
steps.heading: A market that wakes at midnight

paras.text: Under the old bridge, the city’s produce market does most of its trade while Hà Nội sleeps. Lorries unload by eleven; by midnight it is at its busiest.

steps.label: Chợ cóc
steps.heading: The market at the end of the alley

paras.text: Most people buy their food nearer home, at a [[cho-coc|chợ cóc]]: a pavement market that appears in the morning and is gone by noon.
On Friday to Sunday evenings the streets in front of Đồng Xuân fill with a night market.

blocks.heading: A city named after its market

paras.text: Before it was Hà Nội, the capital had a nickname: Kẻ Chợ, roughly “the market place”. The capital was a city of markets long before it had a market building. When a French visitor came in 1883 he found no covered hall and no fixed site; markets met in turns every few days, and vendors walked the streets in between.

That changed in 1889. The French moved the sellers of two older markets, one beside Cầu Đông pagoda and one beside Bạch Mã temple, onto a single site at Đồng Xuân. It began in the open air and was soon covered by five long iron-roofed halls behind five arched gables.

blocks.caption: Đồng Xuân in 1926 and in 2018. Drag the handle, or use the arrow keys. After the 1994 fire three of the five gables were kept; the outer two were removed to widen the side streets.

paras.text: Trams ran close by, the Long Biên bridge brought the countryside in, and the railway station was a short walk away. Đồng Xuân became the biggest and busiest market in the city, and people called it Hà Nội’s stomach. Under the roof, riveted steel trusses echoed the bridge across the river.

In 1994 a fire destroyed almost every stall inside. The city rebuilt it as a three-storey hall but kept the front: three of the original five gables still face Đồng Xuân Street, the two outer ones taken down to widen the roads at either side. One account says it reopened the following year.

items.text: Household goods, electronics, fashion accessories, sweets and dried goods.
Fabrics, silk and brocade, sewing supplies, clothing.

paras.text: Walk north to the foot of the Long Biên bridge after dark and you find the market that feeds the other markets. Founded in 1992 on more than 27,000 square metres, it is the city’s largest wholesale market for fruit, vegetables and seafood. Goods are laid out by about eleven at night, trade peaks around midnight, and by dawn it is quiet again.
Much of the carrying is done by women porters, mostly in their thirties to fifties, who start work in the small hours and move loads of several hundred kilos on carts and shoulder poles.

blocks.caption: Vegetable sellers on the deck of the Long Biên bridge.

blocks.heading: The market at the end of the alley

paras.text: Big markets get the photographs, but most Hà Nội households buy their food closer to home. A chợ cóc, a “frog market”, springs up on a pavement, in an alley or along a railway line, sells fresh food to the neighbourhood and disappears. People like them because they are close, the food is fresh, they know the sellers, and older shoppers do not have to travel. A study in four inner districts counted about a hundred of them against twenty-five official markets, within 300 metres of nearly half the population.

The city wants them tidied away. In January 2026 it counted 468 official markets and 231 informal ones, had dealt with 98, and set a timetable for the rest by mid-2027. Researchers have long warned that supermarkets reach only a minority of shoppers, and some renovated official markets have lost both buyers and sellers.

items.caption: A fruit seller with baskets and a carrying pole.
Selling from the street outside Đồng Xuân at night.

blocks.heading: The first sale of the day

paras.text: If you shop early, you may be someone’s [[mo-hang|mở hàng]], their first customer. Many vendors believe the first sale sets the day’s luck. A buyer who pays easily brings a good day; one who bargains hard and walks away brings a bad one. So a seller may give the first customer a gentler price, or press them to buy, and a few will mutter at a shopper who haggles and leaves.
These are beliefs, not rules, and newspapers report that many are fading. They are worth knowing because they explain the moment. If you are first, buy or say no kindly and quickly.

blocks.text: Bargaining is not haggling for the sake of it. In the old village markets, sellers believed a high opening price brought luck, and buyers bargained to reach the right price, not a cheap one.

stories.title: Vietnam’s first university
stories.dek: A temple to Confucius from 1070, and the royal academy that grew up beside it. Five courtyards, walked from the street gate to the school at the back.

sections.text: Văn Miếu was built in 1070; in 1076 Quốc Tử Giám, the royal academy, was founded beside it.

sections.heading: Seven centuries of teaching
sections.text: The academy taught for more than 700 years, until 1802.

sections.heading: Five courtyards
sections.text: The walled site is divided into five courtyards along one axis.
Calling it a “university” is a modern shorthand: it trained scholars for the royal examinations in the Confucian classics.

stories.appliesTo: Văn Miếu – Quốc Tử Giám in Hà Nội, from the site’s official pages, UNESCO and Vietnamese press. Prices and hours from November 2026.

paras.text: Behind a long wall on a busy street west of the Old Quarter is the quietest place in central Hà Nội. In 1070 King Lý Thánh Tông built Văn Miếu, a temple to Confucius. Six years later his successor, Lý Nhân Tông, founded Quốc Tử Giám beside it, a royal academy that taught for more than seven centuries. Vietnamese call it the country’s first university.

That is a modern shorthand. Quốc Tử Giám did not teach medicine or law; it trained young men in the Confucian classics for the royal examinations that chose the country’s officials. At first its students were the sons of the royal family, nobles and mandarins; from 1253, under the Trần, commoners of ability were admitted too. In 2026 the site marks 950 years since the academy opened.

paras.text: The first Confucian examination was held in 1075, a year before the academy itself. Over the next centuries the exams became the road into government. A scholar passed the regional exam, *thi Hương*, then the metropolitan exam, *thi Hội*, in the capital, and finally the palace exam, *thi Đình*, in front of the king. From 1434 they were held every three years. Those who passed the highest were called [[tien-si|tiến sĩ]], doctors.

Quốc Tử Giám was where many of them studied. Its most famous teacher was Chu Văn An, deputy head under the Trần in the fourteenth century, still honoured as a model of learning and integrity. King Lê Thánh Tông enlarged the school in 1483. When the Nguyễn dynasty made Huế its capital, it moved the academy there in 1802, and the Hà Nội site became a provincial school.
You enter through Văn Miếu Môn, a gate of two storeys, three openings and eight roofs. Look at the stone dragons: the pair in front are Lê-period, the pair inside Nguyễn.
The second gate is decorated with carp, a symbol of students striving to succeed. Two small side gates are named for what a scholar needed: Thành Đức, virtue, and Đạt Tài, talent.

items.title: Khuê Văn Các

paras.text: The second courtyard ends at Khuê Văn Các, built in 1805: brick pillars below, a small wooden pavilion above. Its round windows have spokes like rays of light, for the [[khue|Khuê]] star, the constellation of literature. In 2012 the National Assembly made it the symbol of Hà Nội.

items.caption: Khuê Văn Các, the Pavilion of the Constellation of Literature.

items.title: The Well of Heavenly Clarity

paras.text: In the third courtyard a square pond, Thiên Quang Tỉnh, lies between two rows of stone turtles carrying stelae: the records of the royal examinations. Our story on [the stelae](story:st-stelae) tells their history.

items.caption: The pond of the third courtyard, with Khuê Văn Các behind.

items.title: The temple

paras.text: Through Đại Thành gate is the temple itself. The side halls once held tablets for Confucius’s 72 leading disciples. At the end stands the Bái Đường, a nine-bay hall on 40 ironwood columns, under a panel that calls Confucius *vạn thế sư biểu*, teacher of ten thousand generations. A bronze bell cast in 1768 hangs on one side.

items.caption: Inside the hall: red columns and bronze cranes on turtles.

paras.text: The fifth courtyard is where the academy stood. After it moved to Huế the site became a temple to Confucius’s parents, burnt in 1946. Thái Học house was rebuilt there in 1999–2000. Downstairs it honours Chu Văn An; upstairs, the three kings who built and grew the school.

The examinations that gave the place its purpose outlived the academy by more than a century. The last palace examination was held in Huế on 16 May 1919, and King Khải Định declared that the road of examinations ended there. Văn Miếu kept its temple and its stelae, but nothing more was added to them.

In the twentieth century the state took over its protection. The site was listed as a national relic in 1962 and as a special national relic in 2012, and its 82 stelae were named a national treasure in 2015. In 2026 it marks 950 years since Quốc Tử Giám was founded, and 2025 was a record year, with about 1.7 million visits. For the royal city it belonged to, see [Thăng Long, a capital since 1010](story:st-thang-long).

The temple has never stopped being about exams. Students come before their university entrance exams to pray for luck. For years visitors rubbed the stone turtles’ heads for luck, until the wear forced the site to fence them off.

Around Tết, calligraphers set up their tables by Văn Lake and write characters on red paper for visitors’ wishes: learning, good character, luck. In 2026 the spring festival ran for almost three weeks with 35 calligraphers.

blocks.text: Talented people are the vital force of the nation.
blocks.by: From the stele of the 1442 examination, by Thân Nhân Trung (hiền tài là nguyên khí quốc gia)

paras.text: The site opens every day from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. A ticket is 70,000 đồng, half price for students in Vietnam and people over 60, and free for under-16s. On Wednesday, Saturday and Sunday evenings a night tour with light shows tells the story of the academy and the stelae.
Dress respectfully for the temple halls, keep your voice down, and do not touch the stelae or the turtles. The site counted about 1.7 million visits in 2025, so go early.

stories.title: The family altar
stories.dek: Photographs, incense and a plate of fruit on the top floor of a tube house. Why nearly every home in Vietnam keeps an altar to its dead, even where nobody calls themselves religious.

sections.text: Many Vietnamese homes have an ancestral altar holding photographs of family members who have died.

sections.heading: Not tied to one religion
sections.text: Most people in Vietnam keep it up whatever their religion.

stories.appliesTo: Homes of Vietnam’s Việt majority, with Hà Nội examples. Figures come from a 2023 survey and the 2019 census.
stories.varies: Altars, offerings and how often incense is lit differ from family to family, and so does who keeps the altar.

paras.text: Climb to the top floor of almost any Hà Nội tube house and you will find it: a polished wooden altar, framed photographs of grandparents and great-grandparents, an incense urn, a vase of flowers, a plate of fruit, a cup of water. It is the family altar, *bàn thờ gia tiên*, and it is where the living keep company with the family’s dead.
It is also one of the most widely shared practices in Vietnam. In a 2023 survey nearly half of people said they had no religion, yet 95 percent had an altar at home.

items.text: The highest, most central place in the house.
Photographs, an incense urn, flowers, fruit, water.
The 1st and 15th of the lunar month, death anniversaries, Tết.

paras.text: The altar goes in the most central and highest place in the house. In an old village house that meant the middle room. Hà Nội’s town houses are narrow and tall, and there the highest place is the top floor, so that is where most families put it.

Shops add a second, very different altar: a low one near the door, often on the floor, for Thần Tài, the god of wealth, and Ông Địa, the earth god. A scholar quoted in 2026 says it sits low to keep it apart from the high ancestral altar, not because it ranks lower. The 10th day of the first lunar month is Thần Tài’s day. Because the shop altar sits on the floor, the national tourism authority advises visitors not to step over it or walk directly in front of it.

blocks.caption: An ancestral altar in a high-rise flat.

paras.text: The altar holds photographs of family members who have died, and offerings of incense, flowers, fruit and water. At its centre is the incense urn, *bát hương*, often flanked by candlesticks. Before Tết families clean the urn and the candlesticks and set the altar for the new year: a tray of five fruits, flowers, the square rice cake bánh chưng, betel and a cup of water.
In the Old Quarter you can still see where the pieces come from: altars on Hàng Quạt, bronze urns and altar sets on Hàng Đồng, and paper offerings on [Hàng Mã](story:st-paper-offerings).

Some families light incense every day. Most give the altar special attention on the 1st and 15th of each lunar month, on each ancestor’s [[gio|death anniversary]], and above all at Tết, when the ancestors are invited home from their graves to celebrate with the family.

By tradition the eldest son keeps the rites, and after him the eldest grandson. On a death anniversary the family gathers at his house, to honour the ancestor at the altar. That is the custom as it is usually described; families today arrange it in many ways.

blocks.text: Ancestor veneration rests on filial piety, the duty to care for parents and elders in life and after death.
blocks.by: A summary of the Cultural Atlas, our wording

paras.text: The altar rests on filial piety, *hiếu*: the duty to care for one’s parents and elders, in life and after death. It is not tied to one religion. In the 2019 census only 13.7 percent of people said they belonged to a religion; another official count, by the Government Committee for Religious Affairs, puts it at about 27 percent. Either way, most Vietnamese are not members of a religion in that sense.

Yet nearly everyone keeps the altar. Pew Research Center’s 2023 survey found that 95 percent of households had one, in equal shares among Buddhists, Christians and people with no religion, and that 86 percent of people had offered food or drink to their ancestors in the past year. Many Catholics keep an altar to their ancestors alongside their faith.

The same survey shows how much the practice involves. In the past year 96 percent had burnt incense for their ancestors and 90 percent had offered flowers or candles. More than eight in ten families had a family grave, about seven in ten visited it every year, and nearly eight in ten people said an ancestor’s spirit had helped them. The altar at home and the grave in the village are two ends of the same bond; at Tết, families tidy the graves and invite the ancestors home.

blocks.text: Official counts of religious affiliation differ: 13.7 percent in the 2019 census, about 27 percent in figures from the Government Committee for Religious Affairs. We give both.

paras.text: An old custom is for the host to place a guest’s gift on the altar first, as if offering it to the ancestors; in some homes your box of sweets may go up to the altar before it is opened. Leave the altar and its offerings alone, and ask before photographing it. If your host invites you to light a stick of incense, for instance on a death anniversary, it is a kindness to accept.
For what happens at the altar during the New Year, from the Kitchen Gods to the five-fruit tray and New Year’s Eve, see our story on [Tết](story:st-tet).

stories.title: Chùa, đền, đình: which is which?
stories.dek: English signs call them all temples. Vietnamese does not. A guide to the pagodas, temples, communal houses and shrines of Hà Nội, and the four temples that once guarded the city.

sections.text: A chùa is a Buddhist pagoda; a đền honours a hero or deity; a đình is a village communal house.

sections.heading: Lines blur
sections.text: Real places mix them: Ngọc Sơn, a đền, keeps a statue of the Buddha.

stories.appliesTo: Places of worship in and around Hà Nội. Founding dates are often tradition; we say so where they are.
stories.varies: Many sites combine a pagoda, a temple and a communal house in one compound, and the words are used loosely.

paras.text: Hà Nội has about 5,900 recorded relics, from pagodas older than the city to shrines the size of a cupboard. English signs call most of them “temples”. Vietnamese is more precise: a *chùa* is not a *đền*, and neither is a *đình*. Knowing which is which tells you who is worshipped there, who looks after it, and what to bring.
