paras.text: A *chùa* is Buddhist: the halls hold statues of the Buddha and bodhisattvas, and monks or nuns often live there. Hà Nội’s best known is Trấn Quốc, on its islet in West Lake. By tradition it was founded in the sixth century, under Lý Nam Đế, as Khai Quốc, which would make it older than the city itself; the date is tradition, not a finding. Its tall stupa, eleven storeys and about fifteen metres, is recent, built in 1998, and the bodhi tree in its courtyard grew from a cutting brought by the president of India in 1959.

The One Pillar pagoda is the other famous one. The chronicle dates it to 1049, under King Lý Thái Tông, and a legend says he built it after dreaming of the bodhisattva Quan Âm seated on a lotus. French forces blew it up in 1954; what you see now was rebuilt in 1955.
Both pagodas have been national relics since 1962, and in 2012 an Asian records organisation named the One Pillar pagoda the most unique architecture in Asia: a large title for a very small building.

blocks.caption: Trấn Quốc pagoda on West Lake.

blocks.heading: Đền: temples to heroes and gods

paras.text: A *đền* honours someone other than the Buddha: a national hero, a deity, a local spirit. A keeper looks after it rather than a community of monks. Ngọc Sơn, on Hoàn Kiếm Lake, honours General Trần Hưng Đạo and the god of literature, though it also keeps a statue of the Buddha; in practice the lines blur.

Four temples once guarded the four sides of Thăng Long: Quán Thánh in the north, Bạch Mã in the east, Kim Liên in the south and Voi Phục in the west. In January 2022 they were made a special national relic together. Bạch Mã, on Hàng Buồm in the Old Quarter, is the oldest. Its legend says the god Long Đỗ appeared as a white horse, *bạch mã*, whose tracks showed the king where to build the citadel walls. Like many founding stories it does not sit neatly with the recorded dates.
Quán Thánh, by West Lake, holds a great black bronze statue of the guardian Trấn Vũ, cast in 1677 to replace a wooden one and now a national treasure. Sources disagree on how tall it is.

Bạch Mã is also an archive. It keeps 18 stone stelae and 17 royal decrees from the Nguyễn kings, and it has partly revived an old spring ritual. Of the four guardians, Kim Liên in the south honours Cao Sơn, and Voi Phục in the west Linh Lang.

blocks.caption: Quán Thánh temple, guardian of the north.

paras.text: A *đình* is the communal house of a village, built for its [[thanh-hoang|guardian spirit]]. As Hà Nội grew around its old villages, their đình remained, some of them in the Old Quarter itself.

A *miếu* is smaller: a shrine to a local spirit, often by a road, with no clergy at all. A *phủ* is a shrine to the Mother Goddesses; Phủ Tây Hồ, on a spit of land in West Lake, is the city’s best known. Hà Nội has nearly 600 đền, 5 phủ and more than a thousand private shrines of that religion. Our story on [the Mother Goddesses](story:st-mother-goddess) explains it.

Every spring pilgrims go to the Hương pagoda, within Hà Nội, travelling by boat on the Yến stream to a cluster of about twenty temples and pagodas on four routes. In 2026 the festival ran from 18 February to 11 May; 135,900 people came in the first five days of Tết alone, and motorboats were not allowed on the stream that year.

stories.title: Paper offerings on Hàng Mã
stories.dek: Paper money, paper houses, paper cars: a street that sells gifts for the dead, the smoke on festival days, and the monks and officials who would like a little less of it.

sections.text: Hàng Mã in the Old Quarter sells paper offerings and paper decorations.

sections.heading: Burning
sections.text: On the 15th day of the seventh lunar month many people burn votive paper in the street.

stories.appliesTo: Hàng Mã street, the Old Quarter and Hà Nội’s temples, with national rules and Buddhist guidance.
stories.varies: Some families burn a great deal, others very little or none. Temples set their own rules.

paras.text: Walk up Hàng Mã a few weeks before a festival and the street turns red and gold. *Mã* means paper goods made as offerings: [[vang-ma|vàng mã]], paper money, paper clothes, paper houses, even paper cars and phones. Families burn them so that their ancestors, and the wandering souls who have no one, will have what they need in the other world.

It is an old and widespread custom, and an argued one. Buddhist leaders say it has nothing to do with Buddhism; the state asks people to burn only where it is safe; temples are cutting back. This story sets out what the custom is and who says what about it.

items.text: Paper money and paper copies of goods, burnt for the dead.

blocks.heading: A street that follows the calendar

paras.text: Hàng Mã’s stock changes with the lunar year. Families burn paper money for their ancestors on the 1st and 15th of each month; for a death anniversary or the seventh-month festival they add paper houses, clothes and cars. Before the Mid-Autumn festival the street fills with lanterns; before Tết it turns red and gold.

It is not expensive by the piece. At Vu Lan in 2016 a set of paper clothes cost between 20,000 and 200,000 đồng in Hà Nội, and a paper villa or car about 180,000 to 250,000. The cost lies in the quantity some families burn.

blocks.caption: Hàng Mã street in the Old Quarter.

paras.text: The biggest day for burning is the 15th of the seventh lunar month. On that evening the pavements of Old Quarter streets such as Hàng Ngang, Hàng Đào, Hàng Buồm and Hàng Bông fill with small fires, and the smoke, the fire risk and the ash worry the city.

Two different rites fall on that day, and they are often confused. Vu Lan is a Buddhist festival of gratitude to parents. The offering for wandering souls, *cúng cô hồn*, is for wandering souls. The head of Hà Nội’s Buddhist Sangha, interviewed in 2026, called them entirely different, and said the point of Vu Lan is not lavish trays or burning paper money.

blocks.heading: Who says what

Pagodas should not burn votive paper at Vu Lan.

Festival-goers must burn incense and paper only in the places set aside. It does not ban burning.

paras.text: Behind the custom is an old idea, *trần sao âm vậy*: as in this world, so in the other. The dead are thought to need money, clothes and a house, as the living do, and the family that provides them is keeping faith with its ancestors. The researcher Nguyễn Hùng Vĩ, quoted in the Ministry of Culture’s newspaper, traces the burning to that idea.

Buddhism does not share it. In 2018 the Vietnam Buddhist Sangha asked its clergy to guide people away from burning paper at Buddhist sites, and a senior monk said plainly that the Buddha never taught it. The letter is about pagodas, not homes; at home, families decide for themselves.

Fire is the practical worry. In October 2015 a resident of a tower block in Linh Đàm dumped the ashes of burnt paper into a ventilation shaft and set off a small fire; hundreds of households were evacuated, though no one was hurt. In August 2026, at Vu Lan, incense and paper set off a string of cemetery fires in Huế; reports counted between 13 and more than 20.
That is why the rules talk about place rather than belief: burn where it is safe, in the burners that temples and buildings set aside.

blocks.text: Reports differ on the number of fires in Huế in August 2026: Tuổi Trẻ counted 13, Tiền Phong more than 20.

paras.text: In the 2026 festival season Hà Nội’s temples were noticeably stricter. Quán Thánh asked visitors not to bring paper offerings into the main shrine; Kim Liên stopped burning in its main worship area and played reminders over loudspeakers; Phủ Tây Hồ set up a supervised burning place. The city also banned scattering rice or salt and sticking incense into trees. At Kim Liên, the heavy smoke of earlier years has clearly fallen.

paras.text: For a week or so each winter, Hà Nội changes. The flower markets fill the Old Quarter with peach branches and kumquat trees; families clean their homes, cook, and tidy their ancestors’ graves. Then the year turns at midnight, and the visiting begins.

Tết Nguyên Đán, the Lunar New Year, is the biggest holiday in Vietnam. In 2026 state employees had nine days off, from 14 to 22 February; the year began on 17 February. Here is how the days run in Hà Nội, from the send-off of the Kitchen Gods to the third day of the year.

paras.text: Tết starts a week early, on the 23rd day of the last lunar month, with the [[ong-tao|Kitchen Gods]]. In the folk tale, two men and a woman who died in a fire became the gods of the hearth; the story has been passed on by word of mouth and exists in several versions. Each year they go up to heaven to report on the household, and families send them off with an offering, by folk belief before noon.

They travel on carp. Families buy live fish and release them into a lake or river. On 10 February 2026 Hanoians lined the bridges of West Lake and the lake in Nghĩa Đô park to do it. The custom has a problem: people used to throw the plastic bags and basins in after the fish. Before the 2026 festival police in Tây Hồ went door to door asking them not to; bins were set out by the bridges, and volunteers cleaned the water afterwards.

blocks.heading: Peach blossom and the flower market

paras.text: In Hà Nội the Tết flower is peach. Much of it comes from Nhật Tân, where nearly 800 households grow peach on about 80 hectares, mostly on the banks of the Red River. There are two kinds: đào bích, deep red and dense, and đào phai, a paler pink. In 2026 a branch cost from 100,000 to 350,000 đồng, a tree a million or more, and storms had cut the supply.

In the Old Quarter the flowers are sold on Hàng Lược, a market about a century old that runs from the middle of the last month to the afternoon of the 30th: peach, kumquat trees, chrysanthemums, narcissus, and the white apricot that, the Ministry of Culture’s newspaper says, Hanoians have always loved.

blocks.heading: The altar and the five fruits

paras.text: Between the 23rd and the 30th families visit their ancestors’ graves, clean them, light incense and leave flowers, fruit, paper money and sometimes a small kumquat tree. They are inviting the ancestors home. For many Hà Nội families that means a trip to the big cemeteries such as Văn Điển.

At home the altar is cleaned and set with a tray of five fruits. In the north the tray usually rests on a hand of green bananas, with a pomelo or a Buddha’s hand in the middle and fruit of different colours around it. In the south the fruits are chosen to make a wish out of their names: custard apple, fig, coconut, papaya and mango sound like “cầu sung vừa đủ xài”, may we have just enough to spend. These explanations come from popular writing; every family arranges its own tray.
And there is food. Bánh chưng, the square sticky-rice cake wrapped in leaves, is no longer the rare treat it once was, but many families still make it, because Tết does not feel like Tết without it.

blocks.text: Folk explanations for Tết customs, from the Kitchen Gods to the five fruits, differ between sources and families. We give them as explanations people offer, not as history.

paras.text: On the night of the 30th, in the last hour before [[giao-thua|giao thừa]], families make one more offering, often at the main door: sticky rice, a boiled chicken, betel, wine, flowers. According to the cultural researcher Phạm Đình Hải, it sees off the old year’s guardian deity and welcomes the new one. The paper offerings are burnt before one o’clock.

At midnight the sky fills with fireworks. Exploding firecrackers are banned in Vietnam; adults may use quiet fireworks bought from licensed sellers, and cities may put on public displays of up to fifteen minutes. In 2026 Hà Nội fired them from 33 places, eleven of them high-altitude, at a cost of nearly 40 billion đồng.

The first visitor of the year matters. In the custom of xông đất, the first person through the door is believed to bear on the household’s fortune for the year, so families often invite someone in advance: a person of a compatible age and a successful life, who arrives on the morning of the first day with small gifts and lucky money for the children. Some families send one of their own out before midnight so that they can be the first to come back in. Many people now treat it more as a pleasure of the New Year than a forecast.

Children receive lucky money in red envelopes, called mừng tuổi in the north and lì xì in the south. Where the word lì xì comes from is uncertain; one explanation makes it a borrowing meaning profit, another a legend of the Tang dynasty.
A saying sets the order of visits: *mùng 1 Tết cha, mùng 2 Tết mẹ, mùng 3 Tết thầy*. The first day for the father’s family, the second for the mother’s, the third for teachers.

paras.text: Many Hanoians begin the year at a pagoda or temple. On the first day of 2026 crowds filled Trấn Quốc on West Lake and Ngọc Sơn on Hoàn Kiếm Lake to pray for a peaceful year; a reporter noted that, crowded as it was, everyone was quiet.

Others ask for a character. Calligraphers sit at Ngọc Sơn and, every spring, by Văn Lake at Văn Miếu, writing characters for luck, learning and success on red paper. In 2026 the calligraphy festival ran from 11 February to 1 March. Our story on [Văn Miếu](story:st-van-mieu-university) tells more.

stories.title: The lake of the returned sword
stories.dek: A sword from the water, a turtle who took it back, and a lake that kept the story. How the legend of Hoàn Kiếm grew over six hundred years, and the real turtles that lived in it.

sections.text: In the legend, after the victory over the Ming, a golden turtle rose from the lake and asked Lê Lợi to return his magic sword; the lake became Hoàn Kiếm, the Lake of the Returned Sword.

stories.appliesTo: Hoàn Kiếm Lake in central Hà Nội. The legend is a legend; its written history follows Vietnamese scholars.
stories.varies: The legend is told in several versions. Sources differ on the Turtle Tower’s builder and on the turtles’ measurements.

paras.text: Every Hanoian child learns the story. A fisherman pulls a blade from the river in his net; a rebel leader finds a hilt in a forest. Put together, they make a sword that carries the uprising of Lê Lợi to victory over the Ming. Years later, when Lê Lợi is king and boating on a lake in his capital, a golden turtle rises from the water and asks him to return the sword to the Dragon King. He does, and the lake is named Hoàn Kiếm, the Returned Sword.

It is a legend, and like most legends it has a history of its own: it took centuries to reach the form taught in schools today. And the lake did have giant turtles, real ones, until the last of them died in 2016. This story follows both.

items.text: Hoàn Kiếm, “Returned Sword”; earlier Lục Thủy, “Green Water”.
About 10.7 hectares, once much larger.
Built around 1886, about 9 m tall.
Died 19 January 2016.

paras.text: Scholars at Hanoi Metropolitan University have traced the story through the old books. The oldest, *Lam Sơn thực lục* of 1431, the official history of Lê Lợi’s war, tells only half of it: the fisherman Lê Thận netting a strip of iron inscribed with the words “Thuận Thiên”, and Lê Lợi praying that the blade and hilt, if heaven-sent, should fit. There is no lake and no turtle.

The lake comes later. Writers of the late eighteenth century tell of a king who sees a huge turtle, points his sword at it, and throws or drops the sword into the water. In these versions losing the sword is a bad omen, a sign of a dynasty’s decline. The nineteenth-century geography *Đại Nam nhất thống chí* has the turtle take the sword in its mouth and dive.

The version Hanoians know now, with the sword received from the water and solemnly given back to the Dragon King, was strung together in the late nineteenth century, says the researcher Trần Quang Đức, and fixed in modern collections of folk tales and the school textbook. The legend did not shrink with time. It grew.

paras.text: The lake has had many names. Long ago it was Lục Thủy, Green Water. It was also much bigger, reaching from behind Hàng Đào in the Old Quarter down to Hàng Chuối. A road built across it split it into two lakes, Tả Vọng on the left and Hữu Vọng on the right; architects date the road to the early eighteenth century, other accounts later. The navy once drilled on Hữu Vọng.

From 1884 the French filled Hữu Vọng to build their first quarter in the city. What is left, about 10.7 hectares, is the lake you see now. Its formal name is Hoàn Kiếm; in everyday speech Hanoians often call it Hồ Gươm, Sword Lake.

The Turtle Tower was built around 1886 by a wealthy local known as Bá Kim; sources give his full name differently. A story says he wanted to bury his father’s remains on the islet, a lucky site, and that the bones were later thrown into the lake. Hữu Ngọc tells it; another account calls it oral tradition that cannot be verified.

The tower is small, about nine metres tall: two lower storeys with Gothic-style pointed arches, two upper ones with the roof of a Vietnamese temple. An architect quoted by Tuổi Trẻ says that as architecture it is nothing special. It does not matter. Lit at night in the middle of the water, it has become one of the best-known pictures of Hà Nội.

blocks.caption: The Turtle Tower lit at night.

paras.text: The lake really did have giant turtles. One that died in 1967, about 200 kilograms, is preserved at Ngọc Sơn temple. In April 2011 the last known turtle in the lake, suffering from a skin disease, was caught and treated on an islet: it measured 185 centimetres, weighed 169 kilograms, and DNA tests showed it was female.
She was found dead on 19 January 2016, aged about 200 by one scientist’s estimate. German specialists preserved her body, and since 2019 she has been displayed at Ngọc Sơn beside the turtle of 1967.

What species she was is still argued. Most specialists consider her a Yangtze giant softshell, *Rafetus swinhoei*; some Vietnamese scientists named her a species of her own. Either way, the species is nearly gone: as of 2024 only two animals were known, one in the wild in Vietnam and one captive male in China. The last known female in Vietnam died at Đồng Mô lake, west of the city, in 2023.

blocks.text: Measurements of the turtles differ between reports (the 1967 turtle is given as 1.9 or 2.1 m, the 2016 turtle as 1.85 or 2.08 m), probably because they were measured differently.

paras.text: The story is everywhere in the city. Lê Lợi returning the sword is a classic act of water puppetry. At the north end of the lake, the red Thê Húc bridge leads to Ngọc Sơn temple, where the two turtles rest. And every weekend evening, when the streets around the lake close to traffic, families walk the shore the turtle once swam past.
For more about the lake as a place to spend a day, see [a day by the lake](story:st-hoan-kiem-days).

stories.title: Thăng Long, a capital since 1010
stories.dek: A king, a river plain and a rising dragon. How a thousand years of Hà Nội lie stacked under one walled square in Ba Đình, and what you can still see of them.

sections.text: Hà Nội counts its history as a capital from 1010, when King Lý Thái Tổ moved the court here and named the city Thăng Long. The city marked its thousandth year in 2010.

sections.heading: The citadel
sections.text: In the same year the Central Sector of the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long – Hà Nội was added to UNESCO’s World Heritage List.

sections.heading: What you can see
sections.text: Đoan Môn, the gate of the old Forbidden City, leads north along the old axis; nearby are the excavations at 18 Hoàng Diệu.

stories.appliesTo: The Imperial Citadel in Ba Đình, Hà Nội, and the city’s history as a capital. Dates follow the government portal and the site’s conservation centre.
stories.varies: Official sources differ on a few dates (the name Đông Kinh, the French demolition) and on excavated areas; we give both where they do.

paras.text: In the autumn of 1010 a king came by boat to an old walled town on the plain. He had left the capital at Hoa Lư for a site, as he put it, at the centre of the land. The court chronicle says that as his boat arrived, a yellow dragon rose beside it. He named the place Thăng Long, the rising dragon.

The dragon is legend; the move is history. From that year Hà Nội counts its life as a capital, and in 2010 it celebrated a thousand years. In the same year the heart of the old royal city, a square of gates, lawns and excavation pits in Ba Đình, was inscribed as a World Heritage Site. It is one of the few places where you can stand on top of a thousand years, more or less in layers.

items.text: 1010, by Lý Thái Tổ, on the older citadel of Đại La.
Inscribed 31 July 2010.
Đoan Môn, fifteenth century, five arches.

paras.text: Lý Thái Tổ explained his move in a short text, the *Chiếu dời đô*, Edict on Moving the Capital: just 214 characters of classical Chinese. In modern Vietnamese translation it says that, looking across the whole land, only this place is the finest site, a meeting point of the four directions, and that the dynasty should build at the centre for the sake of all the generations to come. It ends not with an order but with a question to the court: what do you think?

Đại La was not empty when he came. It was an old citadel that a Tang governor, Gao Pian (in Vietnamese, Cao Biền), had enlarged in 866, during the long centuries of Chinese rule. The king renamed it. The chronicle *Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư*, compiled centuries later, gives the reason as the yellow dragon by the royal boat; some modern retellings make it a cloud dragon. Either way, the name stuck for most of the next eight hundred years.

The edict itself survives through copies. In 2010, the anniversary year, archivists announced that the oldest known woodblock of it had been found at the national archives in Đà Lạt. Whether it was carved in the seventeenth century or the early nineteenth is still argued.

blocks.text: Looking across our land, only this place is the finest site.
blocks.by: Chiếu dời đô (1010), from a modern Vietnamese translation, our English

paras.text: Thăng Long was the capital of three long dynasties: the Lý, who founded it, the Trần, who repaired the citadel and rebuilt its Forbidden City in 1243, and the Lê. The names changed with the rulers. The Hồ called it Đông Đô, Eastern Capital, in 1397; under Ming occupation in the early fifteenth century it was Đông Quan; after Lê Lợi drove the Ming out it became Đông Kinh.

When the Nguyễn united the country in 1802 they ruled from Phú Xuân, today’s Huế, and Thăng Long became a regional seat. In 1805 it kept its name, but with a different character for *Long*: no longer the dragon, a word that sounds the same and means prosperity. In 1831 Emperor Minh Mạng made it the seat of a new province, Hà Nội, and the province gave the city the name it has today.

blocks.text: Two pages of the same government portal date the name Đông Kinh to 1427 and to 1430. We give both.

blocks.heading: What the French left, and what they did not

paras.text: The citadel you walk through today is mostly a Nguyễn one, built from 1805, on top of the Lê and Lý royal city. It did not last long. In 1882 French troops attacked it; two marks of their cannon fire can still be seen on the brick of Bắc Môn, the north gate. When the citadel fell, its governor, Hoàng Diệu, took his own life rather than surrender. He is honoured, with Nguyễn Tri Phương, who had defended the city in 1873, in the small pavilion above the gate.

After a treaty in 1883 France ruled the north, and a decree of 1888 made Hà Nội a French city. Between 1894 and 1897 most of the citadel was pulled down; Kính Thiên palace made way for an artillery barracks. The Flag Tower, a brick tower of 1805–1812 more than thirty metres tall, survived.

blocks.caption: The Flag Tower of 1805–1812.

items.title: Đoan Môn

paras.text: Enter at the south, through Đoan Môn, the gate of the [[cam-thanh|Forbidden City]]. It dates from the early Lê in the fifteenth century, repaired under the Nguyễn. It has five arched openings; the middle one was the king’s. A dig there in 1999 found a Lê paved yard 1.2 metres down, and a Trần brick road beneath that.

items.caption: Đoan Môn, seen from the south.

items.title: Kính Thiên

paras.text: North of the gate is the platform where Kính Thiên, the main palace, stood: built in 1428, rebuilt in 1465, demolished by the French. A wide flight of stone steps, carved with dragons, survives. Of the hall above it, nine bays wide, archaeologists have found 28 of its 60 column positions. This is the building now being rebuilt.

items.caption: Stone dragons on the steps of the Kính Thiên site.

paras.text: Behind the platform is a plain building. House D67 was built in 1967, and from September 1968 until 30 April 1975 the Politburo and the Central Military Commission met here to direct the war. Its rooms and the bunkers beneath were opened as new exhibitions in August 2025.

At the north end stands Hậu Lâu, the rear pavilion, built by Emperor Minh Mạng in 1821 and remodelled by the French, who called it the Pagode des Dames. The Centre’s own texts disagree about its first use: one calls it Daoist, another says it was for Buddhist worship.

items.title: Bắc Môn

paras.text: A short walk north is the north gate, with its two cannon marks and the shrine to Hoàng Diệu above. Its plaque reads Chính Bắc Môn.

items.caption: Bắc Môn lit at night.

paras.text: In December 2002 archaeologists began digging at 18 Hoàng Diệu, about a hundred metres west of the Kính Thiên foundations. By the end of 2009 they had opened about 33,000 square metres and recorded 168 features: 95 building foundations, 24 wells, 33 drains and the lines of walls, layered from Đại La, in the seventh to ninth centuries, up through the Lý, Trần and Lê to the Nguyễn.

The finds range from the bricks of Đại La, some stamped with the name of the army unit that made them, to Lê roof tiles shaped as dragons, royal ceramics, a boat with its oars, and ceramics brought from China, Japan and West Asia. That depth, one capital on top of another in the same place, is what the conservation centre means when it speaks of over 1,300 years of continuous history.
The site of the new National Assembly building next door was dug in 2008–09 and added more: over 400 of its finds are shown in an underground display beneath it.

blocks.text: Excavated areas are given differently depending on which digs are counted: about 33,000 m² for 18 Hoàng Diệu by 2009 in one Centre text, and over 30,000 m² for that site and the National Assembly site together in a 2025 account.

paras.text: The square beside the citadel, Ba Đình, is where the modern state began. On 2 September 1945 Hồ Chí Minh read the Declaration of Independence there, proclaiming the Democratic Republic of Vietnam with Hà Nội as its capital. War followed. On 10 October 1954 the city was handed over and the national flag was raised at the Flag Tower,.

Through the next war the leadership worked inside the old citadel walls, in House D67 and the bunkers under it. In 1976, after reunification, the National Assembly confirmed Hà Nội as capital of the whole country.

The celebrations began at eight in the morning on 1 October 2010 by Hồ Gươm, with a sacred flame lit, and ran for ten days, with stages set up around the lake. They ended on 10 October at Ba Đình with a 21-gun salute and a parade of about 12,000 marchers; nearly 40,000 people took part.
For [the lake at the centre of those celebrations](story:st-sword-lake), see our story on its legend.

For years the question has been whether to rebuild the palace that the French pulled down. In July 2026 the World Heritage Committee asked Vietnam to keep preparing the technical documents for it. A dig at its base that year found about six metres of layers, from Đại La to the Nguyễn. The city council approved a preliminary budget of 1,686 billion đồng for 2026 to 2030, and work began on 29 September 2026, after what the Centre describes as fifteen years of research.

The citadel is open every day from 8:00 to 17:00. Entry is 100,000 đồng; people aged 60 and over and students with a card pay half, and children under 16 go free. The Flag Tower opened for visitors to climb in early 2025.

On weekend evenings there is a guided night tour, run since 2021, that takes about an hour and a half from Đoan Môn to the excavations; in 2024 it cost 300,000 đồng for adults. If you want to film, ask the site first; and dress neatly, as you would at any place of history.
Give the citadel a morning. Enter at Đoan Môn, walk north along the axis to Hậu Lâu, then walk to the excavations at 18 Hoàng Diệu, and leave the Flag Tower for last.

stories.title: The Mother Goddesses
stories.dek: Goddesses of heaven, water and forest, a fairy who came down to earth, and mediums who change costume a dozen times in a night. The Mother Goddess religion of northern Vietnam, banned for decades and now World Heritage.

sections.text: Many people worship the Mother Goddesses of Three Realms for health and success.

sections.heading: Open to anyone
sections.text: The belief is open to people of any age, occupation or religion.

stories.appliesTo: The Mother Goddess religion of the Việt, strongest in the north, with Hà Nội examples. From UNESCO, the UN in Viet Nam, the national tourism authority and Vietnamese press.
stories.varies: Shrines and rituals differ; not everyone in the north takes part, and many who do never go to a mediumship ritual.

paras.text: In a temple hall the musicians strike up and a medium in costume begins to dance. For a while the medium is a god. Then the costume changes, and another god arrives, and another: one medium may embody several in a single ceremony.

This is [[hau-dong|hầu đồng]], or lên đồng, the best-known ritual of the Mother Goddess religion, *Đạo Mẫu*. Its followers worship the Mothers of Three Realms, heaven, water, and mountains and forests, for health and success. Condemned for decades as superstition, it was added to UNESCO’s list of the intangible heritage of humanity in 2016.

items.text: Heaven, water, mountains and forests.
Liễu Hạnh.
Hầu đồng, with chầu văn music.
Representative List, 2016.

paras.text: The religion honours the Mothers of the Three Realms: of heaven, of water, and of the mountains and forests. Their pantheon draws on the Kinh, the Việt majority, and from the Mường, Tày, Nùng and Dao peoples of the northern hills.

Above them all in popular devotion stands Liễu Hạnh, honoured as Mother of the World. She is told of as a fairy who came down to earth, lived as a woman and later turned to Buddhism, and she is counted among the Four Immortals of Vietnamese belief. UNESCO’s record notes that the religion contributes to the appreciation of women and their roles in society.

blocks.caption: Phủ Tây Hồ, on West Lake.

paras.text: Daily worship is quiet: incense, flowers and prayers at a shrine. The ritual that draws attention is hầu đồng. One medium embodies several gods in turn in a single ceremony, changing costume for each, to the sung music called [[chau-van|chầu văn]] and to dance. The practice is carried by temple keepers, ritual masters, mediums, assistants and musicians, and is passed on mostly by word of mouth.

It is not a performance for an audience, though people watch. During the ritual members of the congregation may come forward to the medium with offerings or requests. A scholar quoted in 2016 criticised the crowding and loud music at some rituals.

paras.text: For decades the state condemned lên đồng as superstition and banned it. The ban was lifted in 1987, and from the early 1990s the practice revived openly, carried by its own followers. Vietnam put it on its national list of intangible heritage in 2013, and UNESCO inscribed it at its 11th session, in Addis Ababa, on 1 December 2016, Vietnam time.

Anyone may take part, whatever their age, occupation or religion. The religion is strongest in the north and north-central regions, with its centre in Nam Định, south of Hà Nội, and is also found in Hồ Chí Minh City.

blocks.text: Sources date the end of the restrictions differently: the ban was lifted in 1987 according to two press features, while the open revival is dated to the early 1990s.

paras.text: UNESCO’s decision names one danger outright: over-commercialisation. Rituals can be costly, and an artisan quoted by Nhân Dân in 2022 spoke of devotees who spent until they were ruined. Since 2018 the Ministry of Culture has asked that hầu đồng be held only at Mother Goddess shrines and relic sites, not as street shows or tourist services, with fewer paper and costly offerings. In 2023 it said such distortions were continuing and even increasing.

The music and costume of hầu đồng are striking, and some have taken them to the stage: in 2016 a Hà Nội theatre ran staged performances. The Ministry of Culture counts staging the ritual outside its proper setting among the distortions it wants corrected. UNESCO’s decision, for its part, stresses what the practice does for its community: it is open to anyone, with no restrictions, and promotes tolerance between ethnic groups and religions.
Hà Nội has nearly 600 đền, 5 phủ and some 1,230 private shrines of the religion. The best known is Phủ Tây Hồ, on West Lake, where crowds gather from early morning on the first day of Tết.
If you come across a ritual, remember it is worship, not a show: stand at the side, keep quiet, and ask the temple keeper before filming.

A phủ is one of several kinds of sacred place in the city, alongside pagodas, temples to heroes and village communal houses. For how to tell them apart, and what each one honours, see [Chùa, đền, đình: which is which?](story:st-sacred-places).

stories.title: Streets named after what they sold
stories.dek: Silver, silk, paper offerings and herbs: how the Old Quarter of Hà Nội wrote its trades into its street names, and what those streets are now.

sections.text: North of Hoàn Kiếm Lake, the Old Quarter is often called the “36 streets”. Each was named after a trade or craft that settled there, and many workshops once made goods for the royal court at the nearby citadel.

sections.heading: Reading a street sign
sections.text: “Hàng” means goods, so the word after it tells you what the street sold.

sections.heading: Then and now
sections.text: Hàng Bạc was the silversmiths’ street and still has jewellers; Lãn Ông sells herbs and traditional medicine; Hàng Mã sells offerings and festival decorations. Most other streets have moved on.

stories.appliesTo: Hà Nội’s Old Quarter: about 82 hectares between Hoàn Kiếm Lake, the old citadel and the Red River dyke, as the city defines it.
stories.varies: Shops change fast and most streets no longer sell what their names say. Dates for some events differ between sources, and a few stories here are legend; the text says which.

paras.text: Walk north from Hoàn Kiếm Lake and the city closes in. The streets narrow, shopfronts shrink to the width of a doorway, and the blue street signs keep beginning with the same word: [[hang|Hàng]]. Hàng Bạc, Hàng Đào, Hàng Mã, Hàng Gai. Read them one after another and they become a list of goods, as if someone had written the stock of an old market across the map. That is close to what happened.

This is the Old Quarter, ~Phố cổ~, the oldest trading district of Hà Nội. For centuries it was the commercial town beside the royal citadel: craftspeople and merchants who made, dyed, cast and sold what the court and the city needed. People still call it the “36 streets”, ~36 phố phường~. The number is a figure of speech. The city’s own regulation counts 79 streets on about 82 hectares, between Hoàn Kiếm Lake, the old citadel and the Red River dyke.

Before the French arrived, Hà Nội had three parts: the walled citadel of the kings, the countryside of villages and rice fields around it, and between them the commercial quarter where most townspeople lived and worked. The quarter served the court first. Its workshops made jewellery, ritual objects, textiles and tools, and its markets fed the city.

It was never one people. Craftspeople came from the villages of the Red River Delta, and merchants from China settled and traded here too; some of the old merchant houses and assembly halls in the quarter were theirs.

blocks.caption: A corner of the Old Quarter today: balconies, shopfronts and trees over the street.

paras.text: The trade streets grew from a simple pattern. Families from one craft village came to the capital to sell their work and settled side by side, so neighbours made the same thing. Each group formed a [[phuong|phường]], a quarter with its own craft and customs, and often its own communal house, a [[dinh|đình]], where the founder of the craft was honoured.

For a customer this made the city legible. If you wanted a silver bracelet you went to the silversmiths; a sleeping mat, to the mat sellers; paper offerings for the ancestors, to the paper makers. The street took its name from the goods: **Hàng**, goods or wares, followed by the thing itself.

paras.text: Hàng Bạc shows the pattern best, because its history is unusually well remembered. In the fifteenth century, under King Lê Thánh Tông, a mandarin named Lưu Xuân Tín came from Châu Khê, a silversmith village in what is now Hải Dương. He brought craftsmen from home to cast silver ingots for the capital, which served as money, and set up the workshop at what is now No. 58 Hàng Bạc.

When the Nguyễn kings moved the court to Huế in the early nineteenth century, the casting of ingots went with them. The Châu Khê families did not. They stayed and turned to jewellery, and silversmiths from Định Công and Đồng Xâm joined them. Because the street handled precious metal, it also handled money: for centuries merchants came here to change and weigh it, and in the 1890s the French called Hàng Bạc *rue des Changeurs*, the money changers’ street.

The guild built a communal house on the street, [[dinh|đình]] Kim Ngân, “gold and silver”, which honours the founder of the hundred crafts. It was ranked a national relic in 2012, and it is still used: in late 2025 it held an exhibition where craftsmen showed how silver leaf is laid and how a sheet of metal is beaten into relief.

blocks.caption: Hàng Bạc, rue des Changeurs, photographed by André Salles in 1896, and the same street in 2023. Drag the handle, or use the arrow keys. The same street, not the same viewpoint.

paras.text: Today the street is lined with jewellers and gold shops, their signs crowded with the words [[vang|vàng]] and [[bac|bạc]], and some still change money. Hàng Bạc is one of the few streets whose name still describes its shops.

Hàng Mã also still does what its name says. Its shops sell paper offerings, the paper money, clothes and houses that families burn for their ancestors, and before the Mid-Autumn Festival and Tết the street turns red and gold with lanterns and decorations. Lãn Ông, named after the eighteenth-century physician Hải Thượng Lãn Ông, is still the street of traditional medicine: the smell of dried roots and herbs reaches you before the shops do.

Most streets have moved on. Hàng Gai once sold hemp rope and sacking; now it sells silk, embroidery and made-to-measure clothes. Others sell shoes, toys, coffee or rooms for the night whatever the word on the sign. The names have outlived the trades, and that is part of their value: together they are a map of how the city used to work.

paras.text: The buildings explain the streets as much as the names do. The typical house is a [[nhaong|nhà ống]], a tube house: a front only a few metres wide that runs far back from the street, through rooms and small open courtyards that bring in light and air. The shop sits at the front, the workshop and the family behind and above.

Street frontage was what a trader needed, so houses grew upward and backward instead of outward. Many of the façades you see are later: under French rule the city around the quarter was replanned with grid streets and villas, and the quarter kept its tube houses behind newer fronts.

These houses are now protected by rule as well as by habit. Hà Nội’s 2013 regulation for the quarter describes its housing as tube-shaped with inner courtyards and sloping tiled roofs, and requires that form, the courtyards and buildings from before 1954 to be kept. It allows no large shopping centres, and no new housing that would add to the number of people living there.

blocks.caption: Tube houses: narrow fronts, built upward as families grew.

blocks.heading: The white horse of Hàng Buồm

paras.text: Among the shops of Hàng Buồm stands Bạch Mã, the temple of the White Horse. It is the eastern of the four guardian temples that were said to protect Thăng Long, one for each direction, and it worships the god Long Đỗ, the guardian spirit of the capital.

Its story is a legend, and is told as one. When King Lý Thái Tổ moved his capital here in 1010, the walls he built kept collapsing. He prayed at the temple of Long Đỗ, and a white horse came out of it; the king built along its tracks, and the walls held. The legend is recorded in a fourteenth-century collection of stories about spirits, the *Việt điện u linh tập*. The buildings you see are mostly nineteenth-century, and the temple was ranked a special national relic in 2022. Its festival falls on the 12th and 13th days of the second lunar month.

At the eastern edge of the quarter, where Hàng Chiếu meets the road along the dyke, stands **Ô Quan Chưởng**. An [[o|ô]] is a gate in the outer wall of the city. Early-nineteenth-century geographies count 21 of them; maps from 1831 onward show 15 or 16. This is the only one still standing.

It was built in 1749, when the outer wall was rebuilt under Lord Trịnh Doanh, and was first called Đông Hà Môn, the gate of Đông Hà ward; the characters are still above the central arch. Accounts of its later rebuilding differ: one gives repairs in 1785 and a rebuilding in 1804, the national tourism authority gives 1817.

The name everyone uses is explained in more than one way. The best-known story says it remembers a military commander, a *chưởng cơ*, who held the gate against the French when they attacked Hà Nội in 1873 and died there. Other explanations tie it to an official who lived nearby or kept watch over the river traffic. The sources agree on the gate, not on the story.

Look closely as you pass under it. It has two storeys, three arches below and a lookout above, built of large bricks left bare, and its heavy wooden doors are still there. On the wall of the main arch is a stone tablet put up in 1881 by the governor Hoàng Diệu, ordering the guards not to harass people passing through. Under French rule the gate was nearly demolished; one account credits French scholars of the École française d’Extrême-Orient with saving it in 1906, a local tradition credits residents who refused to sign for its removal.

stories.title: Life on the pavement
stories.dek: A teapot, some glasses, a few plastic stools: the city’s smallest meeting place, and the long argument over who the pavement is for.

sections.text: A trà đá stall needs little more than a kettle, a teapot, glasses and a few low plastic stools on the pavement.

sections.heading: Who sits there
sections.text: Customers come from every walk of life, from morning until late, to drink, watch the street and pass on news.

sections.heading: Pavements are changing
sections.text: Since December 2025 Hà Nội has been clearing pavements, with fines and surveillance cameras, so stalls are fewer in the centre.

stories.appliesTo: Hà Nội’s pavements, especially in the central wards where the 2025–26 campaign began.
stories.varies: Rules on pavement use are changing, and enforcement differs from street to street. Fines and plans here are as reported up to November 2026; drafts are marked as drafts.

paras.text: An iced-tea stall, [[tra-da|trà đá]], is the cheapest seat in the city. A kettle or a thermos, a teapot, a tray of glasses, a jar of sweets, and a stack of plastic stools a hand’s width high. That is the whole business.

On most Hà Nội streets the pavement is shop floor, car park, kitchen and dining room before it is a footpath. A survey of 120 streets in 2025 found more than nine in ten taken up by business or parking.

steps.label: The vendors
steps.heading: A shop on a shoulder pole

paras.text: Many of the sellers walk in from the countryside. Researchers who interviewed 305 vendors found most were women, and the mobile ones carried up to 45 kilos on a bamboo pole.

steps.label: The rules
steps.heading: And the city wants it back

paras.text: Since December 2025 Hà Nội has been clearing its pavements again, this time with cameras that send the fine afterwards.

Sit down on a stool at a trà đá stall and you are about a foot off the ground, knees high, a glass of pale green tea with a lump of ice in your hand. The stall owner, usually a woman, knows the regulars by name. Behind you a shop is open; in front of you motorbikes slide past close enough to touch. Nobody minds how long you stay.

The stalls are busy from early morning until late at night, and the customers are anyone at all: motorbike-taxi drivers between fares, office workers after lunch, students, retired men who meet at the same corner every morning. Writers on the city keep coming back to the same point. If you want to know what is happening in a street, ask the woman who sells the tea.

items.caption: Stools under a tree on Tú Mỡ Street, March 2026.
A flower seller’s bicycle in the Old Quarter.

items.text: Iced green tea, poured from a pot of cheap local tea over ice. Hot tea, *trà nóng*, in winter.
Sunflower seeds, cracked between the teeth while you talk.
Peanut brittle from the jar on the tray.
The long bamboo water pipe some stalls keep for customers.

paras.text: Ice is newer than tea. One history traces it to an ice factory the French set up on Trần Nhật Duật Street to supply their troops, hotels and bars, and says Hanoians were putting ice in their drinks by the early 1920s. Another says iced tea did not become a northern habit until after 1975, and spread through Hà Nội in the 1990s. Both can be partly true: ice came early, the cheap glass on every corner came later. A glass once cost as little as 500 đồng.

The tea stall is the fixed end of a much larger trade. Since the [[doimoi|Đổi Mới]] reforms of 1986 opened the economy, street selling, done mostly by women, has grown into one of the ways the city feeds itself. Fruit, flowers, bread, sticky rice and household goods move through the streets on bicycles and shoulder poles.

Geographers who spent eight months with 305 vendors found that most of the mobile sellers were migrants from farming households who came to the city for the season, while most of the fixed stalls belonged to people who lived on the street. A full shoulder-pole load could weigh 45 kilos. For the migrants, keeping on the move was not just a way to find customers; it was a way to stay in the city at all.

blocks.text: Without vendors, I don’t think Hanoi is Hanoi anymore.

items.text: A three-step plan begins on 10 March. By May, ramps, parked motorbikes and tea sellers are back.

items.text: The city’s plan, issued on 10 December, starts on the 13th: first persuasion, then inspection, then patrols.

items.title: Fines by camera

items.title: Drafts for what comes next
items.text: Higher fines from 2027 and a scheme to lease pavement back to traders are both put forward as drafts.

paras.text: The current campaign is the most organised yet. Plan 332, issued by the city on 10 December 2025, began at seven in the morning three days later and ran in stages: a month of surveys and voluntary clearing, then inspection and fines across the city, then patrols to stop the stalls returning. Its stated aim was to end informal street markets and change what officials called outdated habits.

What made it different was the camera. From January 2026 fines could be issued afterwards from images, without a police officer on the street; in the first week, police handled about 848 cases, a third of them found by cameras. AFP counted nearly 2,000 surveillance cameras in use. It started in the centre, in the wards of Hoàn Kiếm, Cửa Nam and Ba Đình: Hàng Mã, Hàng Đào, Tràng Tiền, the streets around the lake.

The fines are not small. A business that blocks the pavement can be fined up to 6 million đồng. For vendors, the reports disagree by a factor of ten: AFP gave 250,000 đồng, VnExpress 2.5 million with the goods taken. By June, state media had counted more than 3,000 fines.

blocks.text: Two newspapers, two vendor fines: 250,000 đồng and 2.5 million. They may describe different offences, or one may have an extra zero. We give both rather than guess.

paras.text: Stalls did not vanish; they moved a few metres. Reporters followed them. A bún riêu stall on Hàng Cháo retreated into an alley a metre wide, and its owner now sits at the mouth of it calling customers in; her sales fell to about a third. An iced-tea seller moved onto a neighbour’s porch. A sticky-rice seller rented a shop and saw her rent double. A flower seller who had worked the same paving slab for ten years was moved to an empty lot and lost about half her takings.

Opinion is divided, and not along the lines you might expect. The government reports central pavements noticeably less crowded and fewer repeat offences. Residents interviewed in the Old Quarter said moving tables indoors felt strange at first, but many liked having room to walk. Café owners point out that a good share of their customers want to sit outside.

blocks.caption: A junction in the Old Quarter: parked scooters fill the pavement in front of the shops.

paras.text: Every campaign before this one faded within months. Whether this one lasts may depend on what the city offers in return. In May 2026 two drafts were on the table: one would raise fines for using pavements to sell food or goods to 4–6 million đồng from 2027; the other would let traders lease pavement back, for 20,000–45,000 đồng per square metre a month, on streets wide enough to keep a metre and a half clear and only where half the households agree. An economist quoted by VnExpress suggested trying designated vending zones. None of these was final when we checked.

Pull up a stool where the owner points, order *một trà đá*, and pay what the people next to you pay; it is rarely more than the price of a bottle of water. If the stall you remember has gone from the pavement, look in the nearest alley or doorway. It may have moved, not closed.
If you want to photograph the people at a stall, ask first; our story [Asking before a photo](story:st-photo-ask) explains how.

stories.dek: Tai chi at dawn, a red bridge, a tower on an island and, on weekend nights, a city centre without engines: a day around Hoàn Kiếm Lake.

sections.text: From around 5 a.m. people gather by Hoàn Kiếm Lake to walk, dance and practise tai chi.

stories.appliesTo: Hoàn Kiếm Lake and the streets around it, in the heart of Hà Nội between the Old Quarter and the French quarter.
stories.varies: Walking-street hours change for holidays and events, and the low-emission zone is a pilot. Temple hours and prices are as last reported. The sword story is a legend.

paras.text: Before it is light, the lake already has company. Walkers come first, then the joggers, then groups who set up a speaker on the pavement and dance. By six there is tai chi under the trees and men doing push-ups against the railings. The water is still green and flat, the island tower dark in the middle of it. The traffic has not started yet.

Hoàn Kiếm Lake, [[ho|Hồ]] Hoàn Kiếm, is the centre of Hà Nội in every sense: the Old Quarter to its north, the French-built streets to its south. People simply call it Hồ Gươm, Sword Lake. It is small, a loop of about a kilometre and a half, and it is where the city comes to breathe.

The name comes from a legend every Vietnamese child learns. Lê Lợi, a landowner from Lam Sơn, found a sword that carried him through ten years of war against the Ming. After he won and became king, he was out on the lake in a boat when a giant turtle rose from the water, took the sword in its mouth and dived. The king understood the sword had only been lent. The lake, until then called Lục Thủy, Green Water, has been Hoàn Kiếm, the Returned Sword, ever since.
It is a legend, and the sources that tell it say so. The tourism authority places it in 1428; the government’s own history page says only the fifteenth century.

blocks.caption: The Thê Húc bridge to Jade Island and Ngọc Sơn Temple.

paras.text: At the northern end, a curved red wooden bridge, Thê Húc, often translated as Light of Dawn, leads to a small island and Ngọc Sơn Temple, the Temple of the Jade Mountain. It honours two figures: Trần Hưng Đạo, the general who defeated the Mongol invasions in the thirteenth century, and Văn Xương, a patron of literature and exams.

The site has changed hands more than once. A temple to Guan Yu stood here first. In 1841 it passed to a charitable society, the Association of Good Deeds, and in the middle of the century the scholar Nguyễn Văn Siêu led its rebuilding. Sources date that work to 1859–1862 or to 1865. On the shore he left the Pen Tower, a stone column topped like a brush tip, inscribed *Tả thanh thiên*: writing on the blue sky.

items.caption: Inside Ngọc Sơn Temple.
The bridge lit red at night.

paras.text: The small tower on the islet in the middle of the lake is newer than it looks. It was built in the 1880s, under French rule, by a local notable. One account names him Nguyễn Ngọc Kim and says he put it up as a pretext to bury his parents’ remains on the island, a plan the neighbours foiled. Before that the mound had held a pavilion of King Lê Thánh Tông and a temple of the Trịnh lords.

Look at it closely and it is a mixture: Gothic pointed arches in the brick storeys, a Vietnamese curved roof on top. It has become the lake’s symbol, and the city’s, but the sources disagree on almost every detail about it, from the builder’s middle name to the number of storeys.

blocks.caption: The Turtle Tower on its islet.

paras.text: The lake really did have giant turtles. The last one known to live there, a huge softshell that Hanoians called Cụ Rùa, great-grandfather turtle, was found dead on the afternoon of 19 January 2016. When scientists measured it in 2011 it was 185 centimetres long and weighed 169 kilos. Officials blamed old age and the cold.

Its body went first to Ngọc Sơn Temple and then to the national museum of nature. In the temple you can still see preserved turtles from the lake, including one 2.1 metres long that was found in 1967.

paras.text: On the evening of 1 September 2016, the city closed the streets around the lake to traffic for the first time. Since then, from seven on Friday evening to midnight on Sunday, about fifteen streets, among them Đinh Tiên Hoàng, Hàng Khay, Tràng Tiền and Lê Thái Tổ, belong to people on foot. By 2023 the walking space drew 25,000 to 35,000 people a weekend, and up to 50,000 at Tết.

In July 2026 the same hours took on a second job. The lake and the Old Quarter night-market streets became the first phase of a low-emission pilot zone: from 7 p.m. to midnight, Friday to Sunday, motorbikes and cars are kept out of a dozen streets, and residents push their bikes home. The bigger plan, to limit petrol motorbikes across the whole inner ring road, has been pushed back to 2028.

blocks.heading: “Excuse me, can I practise my English?”

paras.text: Sit on a bench at the weekend and a child with a clipboard may appear beside you, a parent or teacher hovering behind, ready with questions: where are you from, what is your name, do you like Vietnamese food. The habit is decades old. Students once came on their own; now teachers and parents send younger children.

Not everyone in Hà Nội approves. One writer in VnExpress argued that these short conversations teach little and can leave visitors uneasy; readers wrote back to say they enjoyed them. A few minutes is a kind gift. A polite no is fine too.
Come twice: once at dawn for the exercise and the quiet water, and once on a weekend evening for the walking street. The full loop takes about twenty minutes at a stroll.

Ngọc Sơn Temple was open from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. on weekdays and until 9 p.m. at weekends when last reported, with a 50,000 đồng ticket and free entry for children under 16. Dress as you would for any place of worship, and ask before photographing people at prayer; our story [Asking before a photo](story:st-photo-ask) explains how.

stories.title: A bowl of phở
stories.dek: A street snack from a pole-carried kitchen became Hà Nội’s breakfast, then national heritage. A hundred and twenty years of phở, and how to order a bowl today.

sections.text: Phở began as a street snack in early twentieth-century Hà Nội: rice noodles in a clear broth with beef or chicken.

sections.heading: Heritage in a bowl
sections.text: In August 2024 the folk knowledge of Hà Nội phở was listed as national intangible cultural heritage. A 2023 survey counted nearly 700 shops.

sections.heading: Not only Hà Nội
sections.text: Phở Nam Định was listed the same week, and southern phở is served quite differently.

stories.appliesTo: Phở as it is sold and eaten in Hà Nội. Prices are from 2025.
stories.varies: Every shop has its own broth. Phở in Nam Định and in the south is made and served differently, and where phở began is still argued over.

paras.text: Before seven in the morning, the phở shops of Hà Nội are already full. People sit on low stools with their knees near their chins, steam rising past their faces, a pot of broth bubbling at the door. It is the city’s breakfast: most shops sell until about ten and then close.

A bowl is simple to describe: flat rice noodles in a clear, fragrant broth, with beef or chicken. Its history is not. Nobody agrees on where phở was born, and the question still starts arguments between Hà Nội and Nam Định. What is not in doubt is that it grew up on the streets of this city in the first years of the twentieth century, and that it has outlived wars, rationing and a hundred years of change.

items.text: Flat rice noodles in clear broth, with beef (phở bò) or chicken (phở gà).
Mostly breakfast. Many shops close by mid-morning.
About 35,000–40,000 đồng a bowl in 2025; more at famous shops.

paras.text: There are four main stories, and Nhân Dân, the Party newspaper, admits that none has been proven. One traces phở to *bún xáo trâu*, a buffalo noodle soup from Thanh Trì on the edge of the city, with beef replacing buffalo once the French raised cattle nearby. A second points to the French *pot-au-feu*, a beef stew; the paper doubts it, since pot-au-feu was full of carrots and turnips. A third places the first phở in Vân Cù, a village in Nam Định province, and a fourth hears the name in the cry of Cantonese vendors selling *ngưu nhục phấn*, beef with rice noodles.

The heritage dossier submitted for Hà Nội takes a different view: that phở was made collectively, by many cooks, in early twentieth-century Hà Nội, out of all of these influences. The earliest firm evidence fits that. Drawings made by the Frenchman Henri Oger in 1908–09 show a phở cart in the street, and by 1933 a dictionary was defining phở chín and phở tái.

Nam Định has its own claim. Its villages still send hundreds of phở cooks around the country, and its newspapers call the province the home of the trade. The researcher Trịnh Quang Dũng argues the other way: that phở was sold in Hà Nội at least fifteen years before the first shop opened in Nam Định. Both sides have their evidence. This story is about Hà Nội, but it does not take sides.

blocks.heading: From the shoulder pole to the shop

paras.text: The first phở cooks carried their kitchens. A *gánh*, a shoulder pole, held a pot of broth over a small fire at one end and the bowls, noodles and meat at the other. Many of the city’s best-known shops began like this, as a stall carried through the Old Quarter or set down by the lake, before they had an address.

By the 1930s phở had moved indoors. The writer Vũ Bằng described three ways to buy it: from a cart, from a pole, or in a shop. Nguyễn Tuân, in his essay “Phở”, noticed that shops were known by a single word, the owner’s nickname, as if everyone in the city knew them personally. Many shops are still named that way.

blocks.caption: Beef phở with spring onion and herbs.

paras.text: During the war years and the [[baocap|subsidy era]] that followed, private trade in rice goods was banned and the family stalls disappeared. What was left was state phở, sold in state-run shops on streets such as Hàng Bài, Ngô Quyền and Hàng Buồm. You bought a ticket at a counter, queued at the kitchen window and carried your own bowl. A writer who grew up then remembers phở as a luxury, eaten with vinegar because there were no limes.

When there was no beef, the shops still sold the noodles and broth. Hanoians called it *phở không người lái*, “pilotless phở”. The phrase is remembered differently: one researcher uses it for the queue-and-carry system instead.

blocks.text: We could not confirm where the nickname came from beyond memoirs. Sources agree on the phrase, not on exactly what it described.

blocks.heading: Hà Nội phở and southern phở

paras.text: After 1954, when many northerners moved south, phở went with them, and in Saigon it changed. Today the two are easy to tell apart. A Hà Nội bowl is about the broth: clear, savoury, with few herbs. Hoisin sauce, which would cloud it, is rarely used. On the table you will find lime and a jar of garlic and chilli in vinegar, to adjust it as you like, and sometimes [[quay|quẩy]], fried dough, to dip.

In the south the broth is darker and sweeter, and the bowl comes with a basket of basil, sawtooth herb and bean sprouts, plus bottles of hoisin and chilli sauce. Neither is the wrong way to eat phở. They are two cities’ ideas of the same dish.

paras.text: On 9 August 2024 the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism listed the folk knowledge of Hà Nội phở as national intangible cultural heritage. What is listed is not one recipe but the know-how: the bones and spices, the way the broth is kept clear, the habits of the people who make and eat it. The certificate was handed to the city on 29 November that year, at the opening of a festival of Hà Nội food.

Before the listing, the city’s culture department surveyed 18 of its districts and counted nearly 700 phở shops, with the most in Long Biên (93), Thanh Xuân (56) and Hoàn Kiếm (32). The count included only shops that met hygiene standards, so the real number is higher. Phở Nam Định was listed in the same week; its province counts about 300 shops of its own and sends about 600 cooks around the country.

In 2026 the city began preparing a dossier to put phở forward to UNESCO. Experts warn that it has to show something alive, cooked and eaten by a community, not only a famous dish; dossiers usually take about two years, and many are not accepted.

blocks.text: The dossier must show that this is a heritage living in the community.
blocks.by: Dr Lê Thị Minh Lý, heritage expert, to VietnamPlus (2026), our translation

paras.text: Go early. Phở is a breakfast dish, and many shops run out or close by mid-morning. At the busiest places the system can still feel like the old days: at Phở Bát Đàn, listed by the Michelin Guide, you queue, pay and carry your own bowl to the table.
A bowl cost about 35,000–40,000 đồng in 2025, up 15–20% in a year; in the city centre a 30,000 đồng bowl had nearly disappeared. Famous shops charge 50,000–65,000 đồng or more.
Taste the broth first. Then add lime or vinegar if you want to: in Hà Nội the broth is the point, and the cook has already seasoned it.

stories.title: How to eat bún chả
stories.dek: Charcoal smoke at the shop front, pork in a bowl of sauce, cold noodles and a basket of herbs. Hà Nội’s lunch, a president’s dinner, and how to put it together.

sections.text: Bún chả comes in parts: grilled pork in a bowl of dipping sauce, cold rice vermicelli and fresh herbs.

sections.heading: Dip, then eat
sections.text: Take some noodles, dip them in the sauce and eat them with the pork and herbs.

sections.heading: A Hà Nội lunch
sections.text: It is above all a lunch dish, and nobody knows exactly where it began.

stories.appliesTo: Bún chả as it is served in Hà Nội. Prices from 2022–24.
stories.varies: Every shop has its own sauce and pork, and some add fried spring rolls. Bún chả elsewhere in Vietnam and abroad can be quite different.

paras.text: Around eleven in the morning, the side streets of Hà Nội fill with smoke. At the front of a bún chả shop someone crouches over a charcoal grill, fanning it, while pork fat drips onto the coals and hisses. By noon every table is full: a shop on Mai Hắc Đế told Znews it sells five or six hundred portions a day, most of them at lunch.

What arrives at your table can be puzzling the first time: not one dish but four, and nothing to tell you how they go together. This guide explains the parts, how to eat them, and a little of the dish’s history, from a 1943 essay to the night an American president sat on a plastic stool.

items.text: Charcoal-grilled pork in a dipping sauce, with rice vermicelli and herbs.
Lunch, above all.
About 40,000 đồng at a well-known shop.
Cool in summer, warm in winter.

paras.text: A bowl of [[nuoc-cham|dipping sauce]] with the pork already in it. There are two kinds of [[cha|chả]]: *chả miếng*, thin slices of pork belly, and *chả băm*, chopped shoulder pressed into small patties. Both are grilled over charcoal; the pork was once clamped between strips of split bamboo, and today sits on a wire rack.

A plate of cold rice vermicelli, *bún*. A basket of fresh greens: lettuce, coriander, perilla and basil. And on the table, small bowls of chopped garlic and sliced chilli, so you can make the sauce hotter. Many shops also serve fried spring rolls, ordered separately.

blocks.caption: The parts of a bún chả meal: pork in sauce, vermicelli, herbs, spring rolls, chilli and garlic.

items.title: Season the sauce

paras.text: Taste the sauce first. Add garlic and chilli from the little bowls if you like. A classic Hà Nội sauce is roughly one part each of fish sauce, sugar and vinegar to five of water, so it is light enough to drink from the spoon.

items.caption: Chilli, garlic, vermicelli and the bowl of sauce.

paras.text: With your chopsticks, take a small bundle of vermicelli from the plate and dip it into the sauce bowl.
Pick up a piece of pork and some herbs from the sauce and eat them together with the noodles. Tear larger leaves with your fingers.
Keep going, a little at a time, topping up with herbs as you like. The pickled papaya or kohlrabi in the sauce is meant to be eaten too.
As at most small shops, eat first and pay at the front when you leave.

blocks.heading: Lunch, by the smell of the smoke

paras.text: The Michelin Guide calls bún chả a lunchtime staple in Hà Nội, and that is when the shops are busiest. Some Hanoians eat it at any meal, and it was once thought of as a summer dish. Today the sauce follows the season: cool in summer, gently warmed in winter.

Smell leads you there. Grills are set at the front of the shop or on the pavement, and fanned by hand, so the smoke drifts down the street. Go between about eleven and one, and expect to share a table.

items.caption: A full table at a bún chả shop on Hàng Mành.
Bún chả from above: sauce bowls, vermicelli, herbs and spring rolls.

blocks.heading: Baskets, smoke and a scholar’s question

paras.text: Nobody knows exactly when or where bún chả was first made, and stories about its inventor, including one the Michelin Guide tells about a Hà Nội grill master, are legends. What is remembered is how it was sold: from bamboo baskets carried through the streets, before it settled into shops.

In 1943 the writer Thạch Lam wrote about it in *Hà Nội băm sáu phố phường*, his book about the food and streets of the city. He describes the smoke, the fat sizzling on the coals and the fanning, and he gives a visiting country scholar a famous couplet, asking whether bún chả is the thousand-year treasure of Thăng Long. The line is often quoted as Thạch Lam’s own; in the book, it belongs to his character.

Vũ Bằng, the other great writer of Hà Nội food, thought the city’s bún chả was special perhaps because of the basil grown in Láng village, and because its sauce was never too salty, with the vinegar just right.

blocks.text: A thousand-year treasure of Thăng Long: is it bún chả?
blocks.by: A country scholar in Thạch Lam’s “Hà Nội băm sáu phố phường” (1943), our translation

paras.text: On the evening of 23 May 2016, during his visit to Vietnam, US President Barack Obama sat down at Bún chả Hương Liên, a plain shop at 24 Lê Văn Hưu, with the chef and television host Anthony Bourdain. They ate bún chả, drank Hà Nội beer and stayed about an hour. Bourdain posted afterwards that the meal had cost six dollars in total, and that he had paid.

The shop was full for days. It later put the table, plates, chopsticks, beer bottles and plastic stools behind glass on its second floor, and many diners still order the “Obama combo”: a fried seafood roll, a bowl of bún chả and a Hà Nội beer.

blocks.text: Some reports give the shop’s address as Hàng Bàn or Thi Sách. The Michelin Guide’s listing gives 24 Lê Văn Hưu, in Hai Bà Trưng.

paras.text: When the Michelin Guide published its first selection for Vietnam in June 2023, two Hà Nội bún chả shops received a Bib Gourmand, the guide’s award for good food at moderate prices: Bun Cha Ta on Nguyễn Hữu Huân and Tuyết Bún Chả 34 on Hàng Than. Bún Chả Chan on Mai Hắc Đế and Bún Chả Đắc Kim on Hàng Mành followed in 2024, and Hương Liên is recommended.
The prices did not change much. A bowl at Bún Chả Chan was still 40,000 đồng after the award, and that is close to what a good bowl costs across the city.

stories.title: Egg coffee
stories.dek: A bartender, a shortage of milk, and a café that has stayed in one family since 1946. How Hà Nội came to whip egg yolk into its coffee, and how the city drinks it.

sections.text: Egg coffee is thought to have begun in the 1940s with Nguyễn Văn Giảng, who used whipped egg yolk when fresh milk was scarce. In 1946 he opened Café Giảng, which his family still runs.

sections.heading: What is in the cup
sections.text: Egg yolk is whipped into a sweet foam over hot black coffee, often served in a bowl of hot water.

stories.appliesTo: Egg coffee and café habits in Hà Nội. The origin story is the one told by the Giảng family.
stories.varies: Recipes differ from café to café, and many now serve iced and flavoured versions. Coffee in Saigon is a different world.

blocks.label: Photo essay: egg coffee in Hà Nội

steps.label: Since 1946
steps.heading: A sign at the end of a lane

paras.text: The most famous café in Hà Nội is easy to miss: a lit sign at the mouth of a narrow lane off Nguyễn Hữu Huân. This is Café Giảng, where by the family’s account egg coffee began.
Egg yolk is whipped with sweetener until it turns pale and thick. It is spooned on top of a small cup of strong black coffee.
The cup often comes standing in a bowl of hot water, to keep it warm while you work through the foam with a spoon.

blocks.heading: A bartender and a shortage of milk

paras.text: Nguyễn Văn Giảng started working with coffee in 1937, at the Metropole, the grand French hotel near the Opera House. In the 1940s fresh milk was hard to find in Hà Nội. According to his family, Giảng whipped egg yolk as a substitute, and the thick, sweet foam that resulted became a drink of its own.

In 1946 he left the hotel and opened his own café, at 90 Cầu Gỗ in the Old Quarter. In 1969 it moved to 7 Hàng Gai. Giảng died in 1988, and the business later divided between his children: the café that now carries his name, up a lane off Nguyễn Hữu Huân, and another on Yên Phụ.

Like most food origin stories, this one comes mostly from the people who tell it, and the details vary. One newspaper says Giảng worked in the hotel kitchens, not the bar. One English-language report says he was trying to recreate a cappuccino. The food guide TasteAtlas dates the drink to the 1950s. What everyone agrees on is the family and the café. Giảng’s son Nguyễn Văn Đạo has described the original recipe as egg yolk, condensed milk, coffee, butter, cheese and some secret ingredients.

Egg coffee is still a family business. Giảng’s youngest son runs Café Giảng. His daughter, Bích, opened Café Đinh on Đinh Tiên Hoàng, by Hoàn Kiếm Lake, and her son manages it today. Many other cafés now serve egg coffee too, some of them iced or flavoured.

The recipe has travelled further than the family could have imagined. In 2025 TasteAtlas put egg coffee in its top ten Southeast Asian drinks, and in 2026 a Food & Wine survey of more than four hundred experts ranked Hà Nội the world’s second coffee city, with Café Giảng described as the cradle of egg coffee.

blocks.caption: Egg coffee at Café Giảng, with a glass of iced tea.

paras.text: There is no single rule, but most people start with the spoon, eating some of the foam on its own, then stir the rest into the coffee underneath. Keep the cup in its bowl of hot water between sips. The drink is rich and sweet, closer to a dessert than a morning coffee, and a small cup is plenty.

blocks.text: Egg coffee uses raw or lightly warmed egg yolk. If you avoid raw egg, ask before ordering.

blocks.heading: A city that drinks coffee slowly

paras.text: Coffee reached Vietnam with the French: it was brought in 1857 and planted officially from 1888. Hà Nội made its own habits around it. The city’s coffee is traditionally made in a [[phin|phin]], a small metal filter that sits on the cup and lets the coffee drip through, slowly. The writer Nguyễn Tuân would drink nothing else.

Order coffee with milk in Hà Nội and you ask for [[ca-phe-nau|cà phê nâu]], brown coffee: thick with condensed milk, often drunk hot and without ice. *Bạc xỉu*, a glass of milk with a little coffee, is a Saigon drink, its name popularly traced to the city’s Chinese community, and you will rarely see it on an old Hà Nội menu.

Cafés were also where the city’s artists met. Café Lâm on Nguyễn Hữu Huân, open since the early 1950s, was a haunt of painters. Bùi Xuân Phái drew portraits there as gifts while he drank, and works by Phái, Nguyễn Tư Nghiêm, Nguyễn Sáng and Văn Cao hung on its walls.

Walk down Triệu Việt Vương, south of the lake, and you pass café after café: tiny stools on the pavement, people sitting for an hour over one glass. Some are old. Café Thái at number 27 is nearly a hundred years old, and the street’s cafés appear in the writing of Hà Nội essayists who liked to watch the city go by over a phin.

Others sell the past. Cộng Cà Phê began in 2007 in a 28-square-metre room on the same street, opened by the singer Linh Dung and decorated to recall the subsidy era. Egg coffee, meanwhile, has spread from a single family café to menus across the city. At the family cafés the price has stayed modest: about 20,000 đồng a cup in 2016.

stories.title: Water puppets
stories.dek: A turtle rises out of a pool, a boy plays the flute on a buffalo, dragons dance on the water. Behind a bamboo screen, puppeteers stand waist-deep and work it all with hidden poles. How a village art from the paddy fields became Hà Nội’s best-known show.
stories.appliesTo: Water puppetry as played at the Thăng Long theatre and by village troupes around Hà Nội. History follows the national puppet theatre, a 1121 stele and Vietnamese press; visiting details follow the theatre and a 2026 travel listing.
stories.varies: Each guild has its own puppets, scenes and tricks, and kept them secret. City shows run on a daily timetable; a village troupe may put up its stage on the water only for a show.

blocks.label: Photo essay: a water puppet show

paras.text: Beside Hoàn Kiếm Lake, the Thăng Long theatre plays water puppets every day of the year, seven or eight times a day. Most of the audience are visitors.
There is no floor: the stage is a pool of water, the *thủy đình*, in front of a pavilion hung with a bamboo screen. The water hides everything that makes the puppets move.
Musicians and singers sit to one side and carry the story with drums, cymbals and folk melodies. The puppets barely speak.
The figures are carved from light fig wood, which floats, and lacquered in bright colours. They glide, dive and come up again, a golden turtle among them.
At the end the puppeteers come out through the screen, wet to the waist. About 20 of them work each show; some puppets weigh up to 10 kg.

The first time water puppets appear in writing is on a stone. In 1121, under the Lý dynasty that had made Thăng Long its capital a century earlier, a stele was raised at Long Đọi Sơn pagoda, in what was then Hà Nam province south of the capital. Its inscription describes a performance for the king’s longevity. A golden turtle swam out carrying three mountains on its back; immortals appeared; flocks of rare birds and a troupe of auspicious deer danced on the water.

The scene on the stone is already elaborate, which is why historians think the art is older. How much older nobody can say. The national puppet theatre traces water puppetry back to the legendary Hùng kings; that is a tradition, not a record. What the stele does show is that by the early twelfth century water puppets were good enough to be played before a king.

The trick of the art is that you never see how it is done. The puppeteers stand in water up to the waist in a screened pavilion, the [[buong-tro|buồng trò]]. Each figure sits on a long pole or a set of strings and rods that runs under the water and through the screen, so the puppet seems to move by itself. Villages call the mechanism *máy sào dây*, pole and string.

The puppets are carved from fig wood, chosen because it is light and floats, then painted and lacquered so they survive the water. At Đào Thục, a village on the north side of Hà Nội, an artisan takes about ten days to carve a single puppet 30–40 cm tall. The big ones are heavy: at the Thăng Long theatre some weigh up to 10 kg, and a one-metre fairy needs four people to work it. About 20 puppeteers are in the water for each show, in rubber overalls.
It takes decades to become a master.
