paras.text: A traditional show opens with [[teu|Tễu]], a cheerful boy who acts as host and jokes with the audience. In his own story he was exiled to earth for stealing a peach of immortality, which is why he is so pleased to be here.

Then come the scenes, each only a few minutes long. A city show strings together some 15 to 17 of them. Many are village life: a boy playing the flute on a buffalo’s back, farmers planting rice, men fishing, a fox chased away from the ducks. Some are legends, above all the return of the sword at Hoàn Kiếm Lake, where a golden turtle rises to take back a king’s sword. The show ends with the sacred creatures, dragon, unicorn, tortoise and phoenix, dancing on the water. Village troupes have their own lists: one guild in Nam Định plays buffalo fights, swinging, firecrackers and the fairies’ dance.
The legend of the sword is told in full in [the story of Sword Lake](story:st-sword-lake).

blocks.caption: The final dance on the water.

paras.text: Water puppetry was a village art, and each village’s guild kept its own puppets and tricks. They guarded them closely. New members swore a blood oath to keep the craft secret for life; anyone who leaked it was fined a pig and thrown out. The guilds took only men. A Hà Nội newspaper counted only 14 traditional guilds still active in 2003.

Đào Thục is one of them. By the account of its village stele, the craft there is more than 300 years old, founded by a court official, Đào Đăng Khiêm. For most of that time the troupe had no fixed stage: villagers cut bamboo and put up screens on the water for each show. They built a permanent stage only in 2001. In 2023 Đào Thục water puppetry was added to the national list of intangible heritage, and it remains one of the last workshops still carving puppets by hand.

blocks.heading: From children’s troupe to tourist stage

paras.text: The theatre by the lake began modestly. On 10 October 1969 the city set up the Kim Đồng troupe: nine people doing puppetry on dry land for children. It became the Hà Nội Puppet Troupe in 1975 and took its present name, the Thăng Long Puppet Theatre, in 2001.

Today it plays every day of the year, seven or eight shows a day; in 2023 it gave more than 1,600. It has toured more than 40 countries. A news agency that visited in 2018 found it drawing hundreds of tourists a day while few Hà Nội people came.

stories.title: Ca trù: sung poetry
stories.dek: A woman sings old poems to the click of bamboo clappers, a three-stringed lute answers, and a small drum marks the lines worth praising. Five centuries of Hà Nội’s chamber music: how it rose, fell into disrepute, nearly vanished and came back.
stories.appliesTo: Ca trù as sung in Hà Nội and the villages around it. Its form and status follow UNESCO and the Vietnamese Institute for Musicology; its history, scholars and Vietnamese press.
stories.varies: Guilds and families keep their own melodies and styles. Where and when ca trù is sung in Hà Nội changes often; only some venues hold regular nights.

sections.text: Ca trù is sung poetry performed by a singer, a lute player and a drummer.

paras.text: Ca trù is music for a small room. A woman sits on a mat, an old poem in her head and small bamboo clappers in her hands. Beside her a musician plays the [[dan-day|đàn đáy]], a lute with a long neck and three strings. A third person keeps a small drum, and strikes it to praise the lines and turns of voice. UNESCO calls it a complex form of sung poetry from northern Viet Nam.

For centuries it was sung at village communal houses, for entertainment and at court. In the twentieth century it fell into disrepute and nearly died. Today it is on UNESCO’s list of heritage in urgent need of safeguarding, and some twenty clubs in Hà Nội are keeping it alive.

paras.text: The singer, the [[dao-nuong|đào nương]], is the leader. She keeps time on the [[phach|phách]], a small bamboo percussion instrument, and its beat sets the pace for everyone. The lute player follows her. The drum is small; UNESCO calls it a praise drum, and its strokes praise the singer at the right moment.

There are 56 musical forms. *Thét nhạc* opened the singing at a village communal house. *Hát nói*, which appeared in the late eighteenth century, became the best-loved, and its name has nothing to do with speaking, *nói*. Ca trù was sung for worship at temples and communal houses, for entertainment, at the royal palace and in singing contests between guilds.
The word *trù* means a tally. Listeners who liked a singer gave her bamboo tallies as a reward, and the art took its name from them. It was also called *hát ả đào*, after the singers.

Where it began is argued. Villages tell of a founding couple, and Lỗ Khê, north of Hà Nội, keeps a text of its story dated 1476 and copied in 1740; scholars treat these as legends. The earliest documents are poems from around 1500. One, by Lê Đức Mao, was written before 1505; another, by Hoàng Nghĩa Phú, born in 1480, mentions singers in the streets of Thăng Long. A specialist in Vietnamese music at Goldsmiths, University of London, puts its roots probably in the sixteenth century.

paras.text: Under French rule ca trù was sung in the city’s singing houses, the *nhà cô đầu*. They gathered on Hàng Giấy and in Thái Hà, and later on Khâm Thiên and in other suburbs. Many houses employed hostesses who could neither sing nor play the clappers, and the public came to confuse them with the singers. The art gained a reputation it took a century to lose.
Ca trù thrived until the early twentieth century and then declined. After 1945 the shame attached to it persisted. Quách Thị Hồ, the greatest singer of her generation, was reluctant to teach.

items.text: Seven generations of singers and players; Nguyễn Thúy Hòa was Quách Thị Hồ’s best student.

paras.text: The revival began with a few people who refused to let it go. The singer Bạch Vân first heard Quách Thị Hồ on the radio and was captivated. In 1991 she gave a public ca trù performance at Văn Miếu, the Temple of Literature, and a club grew from it. She became its head, she said later, because nobody else dared put their name to it. In 2000 the club held the first expanded Hà Nội ca trù festival.

Others followed. Lỗ Khê, the village with the founder legend, set up its club in 1995 with 54 members. The Thái Hà family, seven generations of singers and players, began touring Europe, the United States and China the same year; a scholar of the music calls its ensemble the finest performers today. In 2006 Nguyễn Thị Chúc, who had grown up in a singing house on Khâm Thiên, founded the Thăng Long club with her student Phạm Thị Huệ.

paras.text: In 2009 UNESCO inscribed ca trù on its List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. The decision found that too few skilled musicians remained, and it advised Viet Nam to invest in people, singers and teachers, rather than in restoring old venues. UNESCO lists the threats plainly: ageing practitioners, long and hard training, low pay, the loss of places to perform, and competition from mass media.

Progress has been reported every few years. By the first report, clubs practising regularly had grown from 20 to 60. In 2022 the Committee welcomed the progress but warned against over-commercialising it for tourists, and asked for every part of it, including the dance, to be passed on. Viet Nam sent its fourth report in December 2025; the Committee examines it at its session that opens at the end of November 2026. Ca trù remains on the urgent list.

blocks.heading: Ca trù in Hà Nội today

paras.text: In 2021 the city had 16 ca trù clubs and 250–300 singers and players. Its festival in September 2025, at the Hà Nội Museum, drew 21 clubs and groups and 105 individual contestants aged from 8 to 86; 22 were under 18, and there were two and a half times as many contestants as at the previous festival. Hà Nội now has 32 honoured ca trù artisans. Students have started their own projects, such as *Tiếng Ca Nhịp Phách* and its podcast.

Before the pandemic, visitors heard ca trù at Kim Ngân communal house on Hàng Bạc, at Quán Đế temple on Hàng Buồm and at Bích Câu Đạo Quán. The most regular now is Bích Câu: the Ca trù Bích Câu theatre gives free classes and a free show every Saturday night, and in 2026 about ten groups from abroad were visiting each month.

stories.title: Folk prints: Đông Hồ and Hàng Trống
stories.dek: Pigs, hens and a wedding of mice, printed in five natural colours on shell-coated paper; tigers and goddesses outlined in ink and coloured by hand. Northern Vietnam’s two great folk-print traditions, one from a village and one from a Hà Nội street.
stories.appliesTo: Folk prints of the Red River delta: Đông Hồ, made in a village of Bắc Ninh province, and Hàng Trống, made in Hà Nội’s Old Quarter. Technique and status follow Vietnamese press reports, including UNESCO’s 2025 decision as reported there.
stories.varies: Each family keeps its own blocks and designs. Ages and origins differ between sources, and village tradition often places them earlier than the records.

sections.text: Đông Hồ prints every colour from woodblocks; Hàng Trống prints the outline and colours by hand.

sections.heading: On the urgent list
sections.text: In December 2025 UNESCO inscribed the craft of Đông Hồ painting as heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.

paras.text: For centuries, families in northern Vietnam bought new pictures for [Tết](story:st-tet). Hung on the wall for the new year, they showed pigs and hens, scenes of village life, legends, goddesses and guardians. Two traditions supplied most of them. One is Đông Hồ, a village east of Hà Nội whose prints are made entirely from carved woodblocks. The other is Hàng Trống, named after a street in the Old Quarter, where painters printed an outline and then coloured each sheet by hand.

Both are now rare. Only a few households still make Đông Hồ prints, and in December 2025 UNESCO listed the craft as heritage in urgent need of safeguarding. Hàng Trống is held by a single family workshop.

blocks.heading: Đông Hồ: five colours from the earth

paras.text: Đông Hồ prints are made in Đông Khê hamlet, in Thuận Thành, Bắc Ninh province. The age of the craft depends on who is asked. Villagers date it to the Lý dynasty in the eleventh century; researchers place the start of printing around the early seventeenth century; the report on its UNESCO listing calls it about 500 years old.

A design begins as an ink drawing, carved into blocks of [[thi|thị]] wood. Each colour has a block of its own. The printer lays the paper on each inked block in turn: red, blue, yellow and white, and last the black block that carries the outline and holds the picture together. Every stage is done by hand.

The colours are what make Đông Hồ unmistakable, and they all come from nature. Blue is from indigo leaves, red from a red gravel, yellow from the flowers of the pagoda tree and from gardenia fruit, white from powdered scallop shell, and black from the ash of bamboo leaves and of glutinous-rice straw. The paper is [[giay-diep|giấy điệp]]: dó paper brushed with a paste containing powdered shell.

blocks.heading: Pigs, hens and a wedding of mice

paras.text: The subjects fall into a few families: devotional pictures, congratulations, history, everyday life and landscape. The best sellers are animals and village life: a herd of pigs, hens with their chicks, a boy playing the flute on a buffalo’s back. Folk tales appear too, the best known being the mice’s wedding.
People bought them for Tết, for the Mid-Autumn festival and for worship. Printing started months before the new year.

By 2025 only a few households in the village still made the prints. Young people were not drawn to the work, the income was poor, and fewer families bought new pictures for the festivals. Bắc Ninh and the Ministry of Culture prepared a dossier, and on 9 December 2025, at its session in New Delhi, UNESCO inscribed the craft of Đông Hồ folk painting on its List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. It was Viet Nam’s seventeenth element on UNESCO’s lists.

In 2026 the craft is still held by a handful of people, among them Nguyễn Hữu Quả, whose family has made prints for three generations, and the Meritorious Artisan Nguyễn Thị Oanh. Young people have started their own projects around the prints, such as *Hồn trên giấy mộc*, Soul on Woodblock Paper.

Hàng Trống is a street in old Hà Nội. Its pictures are said to date from the sixteenth century, and they were made there and on the neighbouring streets of Hàng Nón, Hàng Hòm and Hàng Quạt, mostly in the last months of the lunar year for Tết.

The technique differs from Đông Hồ in one decisive step. Drawing, carving and printing are the same, but only the outline is printed. Each sheet is then coloured by hand with a brush, so no two prints are exactly alike. The paper is *xuyến chỉ*, not the shell-coated điệp of the village.
There are pictures for worship, the Mother Goddess and Saint Trần, and for the new year: the Five Tigers; a carp looking at the moon; four panels of elegant women; children playing blind man’s buff.

Hàng Trống is now held by one family. Lê Đình Nghiên is the third generation of a family from Bình Vọng village in Thường Tín, whose forebears settled on Hàng Trống street nearly a century before 2006. His workshop is on Cửa Đông street. By 2006 the prints were no longer sold on the old streets at all, and most buyers were foreign visitors.

In late 2019 the Hà Nội Museum gave the tradition a large exhibition: 50 works in three groups, worship, Tết and social life, among them two painted on corrugated metal by Nghiên’s father in 1942 and 1943. The report called Nghiên the only person still holding the craft’s secrets. In 2025 he restored the Hàng Trống pictures at Nam Hương temple. On Hàng Trống street itself, a young artist born in 1997, Hoàng Anh Trung, shows bright new work inspired by the prints; it is new art, not the old technique.

stories.title: Bát Tràng: the pottery village
stories.dek: On the edge of Hà Nội, a village has been firing clay for some six hundred years. A guide to Bát Tràng: its glazes, its prize-winning museum, its market, and a wheel where you can make your own bowl.

paras.text: About 14 km from the Old Quarter, a village has been making pottery since at least the fourteenth century. Bát Tràng’s old pieces are in the national museums in Hà Nội, and its new ones fill the village market.
This guide takes you through a day there: the history in its glazes, the museum that has won prizes for its architecture, the market, and a potter’s wheel where you can try it yourself.

paras.text: The village tells its origin as part of the capital’s. When Lý Thái Tổ moved the court to Thăng Long, the story goes, craftsmen from the villages of Bồ and Bát in Yên Mô, in today’s Ninh Bình, settled here to make the bricks and ceramics the new city needed. Another legend credits scholars who brought pottery skills from China. These are traditions.

The records are later. Documents place the village in the fourteenth or fifteenth century, and the oldest Bát Tràng pieces in museum collections date from the fourteenth. Next door, at Kim Lan, archaeologists digging in 2001–03 found material spanning the ninth to the twentieth centuries; Kim Lan’s pottery joined the national list of intangible heritage in January 2025.

The village’s history can be read in its glazes. Blue decoration appeared in the fourteenth century and was everywhere by the sixteenth and seventeenth. Brown was painted on before glazing. Ivory-white glaze appears on seventeenth-century pieces. And the fine web of cracks on many pieces is a technique, [[men-ran|men rạn]], crackle glaze: the clay body and the glaze shrink at different rates. Potters learned to control it deliberately mainly in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

You can follow the whole sequence in one room. In 2023 the National Museum of History in Hà Nội showed 39 old Bát Tràng pieces in three periods: the fourteenth century, the fifteenth to eighteenth, and the nineteenth to twentieth. Side by side, the early blue pieces, the brown-painted ones and the crackled wares of the last two centuries show how the village’s style changed over six centuries. Among them was a seventeenth-century model house in ivory-white glaze.
Bát Tràng is about 14 km from central Hà Nội; sources give anything from 13 to 15 km, more if you measure from further out. Buses, motorbikes, taxis and tour shuttles all go there.

The Bát Tràng Ceramics Museum, open since 2021, is the best place to begin. Its architect, Hoàng Thúc Hào, built it as seven spirals based on potters’ wheels, which also recall the village’s old bottle kilns, in thin concrete faced with reclaimed local bricks and tiles. It stands beside the Bắc Hưng Hải canal. It won a gold prize at the National Architecture Awards 2022–23, and in 2026 Time Out ranked it 17th among the world’s most beautiful buildings.
The pottery market is a short walk away: stall after stall of bowls, cups, vases and pots.
In the village lanes, look for the Vạn Vân old house, about 200 years old, and the village communal house, whose festival was added to the national list of intangible heritage in December 2024.
Many workshops let visitors sit at a wheel and shape their own piece.
Go on a weekday morning if you can, and allow time for a class. Bring a bag for anything fragile.

Bát Tràng’s pottery craft is on the national list of intangible heritage, and on 10 December 2024 the village festival was added too; it was announced at the communal house the following March. In February 2025, at a ceremony in the old Thăng Long citadel, Bát Tràng and the silk village of Vạn Phúc joined the World Crafts Council’s network of creative craft cities.

Bát Tràng’s artisans also helped make one of Hà Nội’s longest artworks. For the city’s thousandth birthday, the journalist and painter Nguyễn Thị Thu Thủy proposed covering the Red River dyke wall with ceramic mosaic. Begun in 2008 and inaugurated on 5 October 2010, it ran for 3.85 km and was made by artists from Vietnam and abroad, by children, and by artisans from Bát Tràng and other pottery villages. An 810 m section of 1,570 m², called *Vietnamese patterns in the flow of history*, holds a Guinness record as the largest ceramic mosaic.
Not all of it survived. In June 2020 more than 600 m at Nghi Tàm–Xuân Diệu was demolished to widen the road towards Nhật Tân bridge.

stories.title: Tube houses and French villas
stories.dek: Houses a few metres wide and many times as deep; an opera house, a bridge and a governor’s palace; a museum that put Vietnamese roofs on French concrete. How two very different cities grew side by side in Hà Nội, and what is being done to keep them.
stories.appliesTo: The Old Quarter and the French-built quarters of central Hà Nội. Building histories follow Vietnamese press, the National Museum of History and an encyclopedia where noted; rules follow city reports.
stories.varies: Dates and architects differ between sources for several buildings, and the story says where. Rules for the Old Quarter and the villas are revised from time to time.

sections.text: Tube houses have a narrow front and run deep behind it.

sections.heading: The French city
sections.text: The Opera House, the Long Biên bridge and the Presidential Palace were built around 1900.

paras.text: Walk from the Old Quarter towards the Opera House and the city changes shape. Behind you are streets of [[nhaong|tube houses]], each a narrow shopfront with rooms running far back behind it. Ahead are wide streets, a pale yellow palace, and the villas the French built for themselves. Hà Nội grew as two cities side by side, and both are still standing.

This story walks through both: how a tube house works, where the narrow fronts may have come from, the public buildings of the colonial city, and the rules now meant to keep them. For the streets themselves, see [the Old Quarter](story:st-old-quarter).

A tube house, *nhà ống*, has a narrow front on the street and runs deep behind it. The front room was the shop. Behind it came an open courtyard to let in light and air, then a back room, storage and the kitchen; upstairs were the family altar and the bedrooms. The form is associated with Hà Nội’s Old Quarter from the nineteenth century.

Why so narrow? The answer most often given is that houses were taxed by the width of their street front, so owners kept fronts small and built back. It is repeated in newspapers and guidebooks, but no historical tax record has been cited for it. It may be true; it has not been shown.

blocks.caption: Narrow fronts at the corner of Đào Duy Từ and Mã Mây.

paras.text: One house shows the plan clearly: 87 Mã Mây. The street is under 300 m long and keeps more old houses than any other in Hà Nội. Number 87 was built in the early nineteenth century; some sources say later. It was a rice business until 1945, then a Chinese family sold traditional medicine there, and in 1954 the state took it over. From 1998 to 1999 it was restored with help from the French city of Toulouse, keeping its structure and objects, and in 2004 it was recognised as a national relic.
Inside, the plan of a tube house is easy to read: shop, courtyard, rooms, kitchen, and the altar upstairs.

The French colonial government’s public buildings came in a rush around the turn of the twentieth century. The Post Office beside Hoàn Kiếm Lake is two buildings, one of 1893–99 and one of 1942. The Opera House was built from 1901 to 1911 to designs by the architects Harley and Broyer.

The palace built for the Governor-General of Indochina from 1900 to 1906 is now the Presidential Palace. Its architect is often named as Auguste-Henri Vildieu; some sources say that is a mistake and credit Charles Lichtenfelder. Visitors may walk in the grounds but cannot go inside.

The biggest work of all crosses the Red River. The Long Biên bridge was built from September 1898 to February 1902 by the French firm Daydé & Pillé and named after the Governor-General, Paul Doumer. It was the first steel bridge across the river, with a single railway track down the middle, and at the time it was thought the largest steel structure in South-East Asia. Sources give its length as anything from about 1.7 to 1.9 km. Many guides say Gustave Eiffel’s firm designed it; that is disputed.
During the war the bridge was bombed many times between 1965 and 1972. On 10 September 1972 spans fell into the river; it reopened in January 1973.

In 2025 France funded a study of how to repair it and what it should become once the national railway stops using it. Late that year it had its largest repair in more than a century, with rusted rivets replaced by high-strength bolts and a new concrete deck; in spring 2026 motorbikes and pedestrians were kept off for two months.

In the 1920s a building appeared that borrowed openly from Vietnamese architecture. Its architect, Ernest Hébrard, also designed the Indochina Finance Office, built from 1925 and now the Foreign Ministry, and he drew it with C. Batteur: a museum for the French school of Asian studies, the École française d’Extrême-Orient.

The museum, named after the scholar Louis Finot, was designed in 1925, finished in 1929 and opened in 1932 at 1 Tràng Tiền. It is now the National Museum of History. Its octagonal main hall rises under a three-tiered roof that the museum compares to the tower of Keo pagoda. The roofs are doubled, with gaps for the air to move, the eaves are wide, and the brackets are concrete. The museum calls it a typical example of the Indochinese style.

paras.text: Both cities are under pressure. In the Old Quarter a 2013 draft regulation proposed limits for the 82 ha area: in a 28 ha conservation zone, buildings no higher than 3 floors, 12 m, on the street front; in the 54 ha around it, 4 floors, 16 m. Inside, many houses are crowded. In 2026, 902 households in Hoàn Kiếm ward, 3,621 people, were living on less than 5 m² each, and the city gave them priority for social housing in 2026–27.

The French villas have a list of their own. In 2022 the city counted 1,216 villas built before 1954, 53 fewer than in 2013, in three groups. The 222 of group 1, the most valuable, are mostly in Ba Đình, 111 of them, and Hoàn Kiếm, 87. The list changes: in November 2026 the city council considered moving two villas, at 68B Trần Hưng Đạo and 62 Nguyễn Du, down to group 3.

options.feedback: It is widely repeated, but no historical tax record has been cited for it.

options.label: It is a popular explanation
options.feedback: Yes. It may be true, but it has not been shown from historical records.

options.label: It is certainly wrong
options.feedback: We cannot say that either: it simply has not been proven.
